Ref: Regulation 34 and 53 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements)

In continuation to our letter dated July 25, 2026 informing about 31st Annual General Meeting 
(“AGM”) of AU Small Finance Bank Limited (“Bank”) to be held on Saturday, September 5, 2026 
through video conferencing or other audio visual means, we submit herewith a copy of the 
Integrated Annual Report for FY 2025-26 including Notice convening the 31st AGM of the Bank and 
Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. 
 
The Annual Report may also be accessed on website of the Bank at following link: 
https://www.au.bank.in/investors/annual-reports.  
 
The Notice of AGM and Integrated Annual Report for FY 2025-26 are being sent by e-mail to the 
members and debenture holders of the Bank who have registered their e-mail address with the 
Depositories/RTA. A letter providing the web-link, including the exact path, for accessing the 
Notice of AGM and Integrated Annual Report would be sent to those shareholders and debenture 
holders who have not registered their email address. A copy of the said letter is enclosed for your 
record. 
 
This is for your information and appropriate dissemination. 
 
Thanking You, 
 
Yours faithfully, 
 
For AU SMALL FINANCE BANK LIMITED

Scaling with 
Intelligence. 
Governed by Trust.
Over the years, we have grown 
from a focused vehicle finance 
institution into India’s largest Small 
Finance Bank, with a diversified 
banking franchise, a growing national 
presence, and customer relationships 
shaped by credibility, consistency, 
and service. 
 
FY 2025-26 marks an important 
phase in our evolution. As we move 
towards becoming a Universal Bank, 
we are entering a new chapter 
with wider capabilities, a stronger 
presence across markets, and a more 
diversified banking platform. Through 
every stage of this journey, our 
approach has remained grounded in 
prudent risk management, thoughtful 
decision making, and the belief that 
sustainable progress is built on trust.
For us, intelligence extends beyond 
technology. It is reflected in thoughtful 
underwriting, disciplined capital 
allocation, data-led decision-making, 
and customer-centric innovation. 
Trust continues to guide how we lead 
and grow as an institution.
Our theme, ‘Scaling with 
Intelligence. Governed by Trust’, 
reflects the philosophy guiding 
our next phase of growth. 
As India’s financial landscape 
continues to evolve, we remain 
focused on building a future-ready 
Bank that stays connected to people, 
relationships, and long-term value 
creation. This Integrated Annual 
Report reflects how we are scaling 
with purpose, and creating long-term 
value through intelligent growth and 
trusted governance.

Overview and reporting philosophy
This is the sixth edition of AU Small Finance Bank  
(AU SFB)’s Integrated Annual Report, prepared in 
alignment with the International Integrated Reporting 
Framework issued by the International Financial 
Reporting Standards Foundation.
The report provides a holistic and balanced view of the 
Bank’s ability to create, preserve, and sustain value over 
the short, medium, and long-term. It reflects how AU SFB 
uses its business model, strategy, governance practices, 
and capital allocation to deliver stakeholder outcomes 
while operating in a dynamic economic, regulatory, and 
social environment.
The reporting approach integrates financial and non-
financial information into a cohesive narrative on 
strategy, performance, risks, opportunities, and outlook.
Reporting period and boundary
This Report covers the financial year April 1, 2025 to 
March 31, 2026. The non-financial information in the 
integrated report largely covers the operations of  
AU Small Finance Bank Limited.
The scope includes:
	
»
All primary business segments, operating 
geographies, and key support functions of the Bank
	
»
Financial performance in line with applicable 
accounting standards
	
»
Non-financial disclosures covering operational, 
environmental, and social performance
Comparative information, where relevant, pertains to 
the previous reporting period (April 1, 2024 to March 31, 
2025). The FY 2024-25 Integrated Report is available on 
the Bank’s website.
Financial and Non-financial 
disclosures
The Report presents an integrated view of:
	
»
Financial performance and position
	
»
Strategic priorities and growth drivers
	
»
Risk landscape and mitigation strategies
	
»
Stakeholder relationships and outcomes
These disclosures reflect interdependencies across 
capitals and show how the Bank’s activities translate into 
measurable outputs and long-term value creation.
Target audience
This Report is intended for providers of financial capital, 
including existing and prospective investors. It also serves 
regulators, customers, employees, partners, and the 
broader community.
Statutory and regulatory 
frameworks
The financial information presented in this report is in line 
with the requirements of:
	
»
The Companies Act, 2013 and rules thereunder
	
»
The Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021
	
»
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and other relevant 
RBI regulations
	
»
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 and other SEBI Regulations

This governance framework ensures that the disclosures 
are accurate, consistent, and aligned with the principles of 
transparency, reliability, and comparability as prescribed 
under the Integrated Reporting Framework.
Transparency and continuous 
improvement
AU SFB remains committed to strengthening reporting 
through enhanced disclosures, improved data systems, 
and alignment with evolving global standards. The Bank 
continues to refine its integrated reporting approach to 
provide deeper insight into strategy, performance, and 
long-term value creation.
Forward-looking statement
This Integrated Report may contain forward-looking 
statements on strategy, performance, and outlook based 
on current expectations and underlying premises. These 
are subject to various risks and uncertainties, including 
changes in economic conditions, regulations, and market 
dynamics, which may cause actual results to differ 
materially. The Bank undertakes no obligation to update 
these statements except as required by applicable laws  
and regulations.

Who We Are
A Journey of Purpose
For millions of Indians, banking was not always 
accessible. Today, over 1.2 Crore customers are 
part of AU Small Finance Bank’s journey, many of 
whom are taking their first step into the formal 
financial system with us. That transformation is 
at the heart of who we are.
Today, we stand as India’s largest Small Finance 
Bank. But more than scale, what defines us is 
a belief we have held consistently over time. 
When we started in 1996, it was simple: every 
Indian, regardless of background or geography, 
deserves world-class banking delivered with a 
personal touch.
Over the past decade, this belief has guided our 
growth. We have built a financial institution that 
stays close to its customers through a strong, 
retail-led banking model that is both inclusive 
and resilient.
Mission
To build one of India’s largest retail franchises 
that is admired for: 
	
»
Making every customer feel supreme while 
being served 
	
»
Aspiring that no Indian is deprived of banking
	
»
Bias for action, dynamism, detail orientation, 
and product and process innovation 
	
»
Globally respected standards of integrity, 
governance, and ethics 
	
»
Being an equal opportunity employer, 
providing a collaborative and rewarding 
platform to all employees

Dear Stakeholders,
As I reflect on FY 2025-26, I do so with a deep sense  
of pride in the way AU Small Finance Bank has continued 
its remarkable journey. In a year marked by geopolitical 
uncertainties, trade disruptions, evolving regulatory 
expectations and rapid technological changes, our 
approach remained clear: pursue growth with discipline, 
strengthen the institution for the Long Term, and stay 
anchored to our core values. The Board remained  
guided by the overarching principle: growth must be 
supported by sound judgement, and sustainable practices 
focusing on ensuring resilience, building trust, and 
responsible conduct. 
Our vision of building a ‘Forever Bank’ continues to be 
guided by the 5-S Framework:
	
»
Sound financial parameters
	
»
Sustainability of long-term value
	
»
Service excellence for customers
	
»
Scalable and secured digital infrastructure 
powered by AI
	
»
Strong governance, risk & compliance guardrails
Sound Financial Parameters
FY 2025-26 was another year of disciplined execution and 
broad-based growth. Deposits grew 23% Y-o-Y to ₹1.52 
Lakh Crore, while the gross loan portfolio increased 21% 
Y-o-Y to ₹1.40 Lakh Crore, supported by growth across 
business segments. Profit after tax rose 25% Y-o-Y to 
₹2,641 Crore, reflecting operating discipline and improved 
credit quality.
Despite continued investments, cost-to-assets improved 
to 4.1% from 4.3% in FY 2024-25, while credit cost 
reduced to 0.96% of average assets from 1.3% a year ago. 
Asset quality strengthened, with gross NPA improving to 
2.03% and net NPA stable at 0.74%. Return ratios also 
improved, with RoA rising to 1.6% and RoE to 14.2%, 
reflecting the quality and sustainability of growth.
The Bank remains well capitalised, with a capital 
adequacy ratio of 18.7%, comfortably above regulatory 
requirements. The Board has recommended a dividend 
of ₹1 per share, representing 10% of face value, reflecting 
confidence in the franchise’s long-term earnings potential.
Sustainability of Long-Term Value
At AU SFB, we believe that institutions endure not 
because of a single strategy, but because culture, values 
and leadership are reinforced consistently over time. For 
this reason, succession planning, leadership development 
and organisational continuity remain important priorities 
for the Board.
During the year, leadership continuity was further 
strengthened through the RBI’s approval of Mr. Sanjay 
Agarwal’s re-appointment as Managing Director & CEO, 
the elevation of Mr. Vivek Tripathi as Executive Director 
and the continuation of Mr. Uttam Tibrewal as  
Deputy CEO, supporting the Bank’s long-term  
institution-building journey.
Financial and digital inclusion remain central to our 
mandate. Guided by Availability, Accessibility, Affordability 
and Assurance, the Bank continues to expand responsible 
banking through branches, banking outlets and digital 
platforms. During the year, over 22,100 financial literacy 
and outreach programmes were conducted, reinforcing 
financial awareness and economic resilience.
Through AU Foundation initiatives such as AU Ignite,  
AU Udyogini and AU Bano Champion, the Bank supports 
youth skilling, women’s empowerment and sports 
education, creating meaningful social impact alongside 
financial progress.

As of March 31, 2026, the Bank had mobilised  
₹2,950 Crore in Green Fixed Deposits, fully deployed 
into green assets, mainly renewable energy projects 
and electric vehicles. With IFC support, we have also 
strengthened climate risk assessment capabilities for  
more resilient decision-making.
Service Excellence for Customers
Customer centricity has been integral to the Bank since 
inception. Early innovations such as monthly interest 
payouts, deposit slip-free banking and true anywhere 
banking reflected a simple belief: banking should be 
easy, accessible and designed around customer needs.
This philosophy has now evolved into a digital-first 
service ecosystem for the Bank’s diverse customer base. 
The AU 0101 app serves as a key engagement platform, 
supported by digital onboarding, omnichannel servicing 
and more consistent customer communication through 
Quadient, a leading global customer communication 
management platform. Video-based onboarding further 
helps familiarise customers with product features, loan 
terms and key disclosures before branch visits.
Customers can raise grievances through voice, email, 
website, mobile app and 24x7 Video Banking.  
QR-enabled complaint registration with multilingual 
voice-note capability has improved access, especially 
in rural and semi-urban markets. Journey mapping, 
feedback mechanisms and data-driven insights continue 
to help address service gaps proactively.
Reflecting this focus, complaints escalated to the RBI 
Ombudsman declined by 9% Y-o-Y.
Scalable and Secured Digital 
Infrastructure powered by AI
Technology is central to customer experience, 
operational efficiency and risk management.  
The Bank continues to invest with discipline across 
digital platforms, data capabilities and cybersecurity, 
while strengthening a reliable, secure and scalable core 
IT infrastructure.
Our focus is on building seamless user experiences  
and transforming operations to make AU SFB  
a future-ready Bank powered by AI, data intelligence 
and cyber resilience. AI-led capabilities are being 
deployed across customer engagement, service delivery, 
underwriting, fraud detection and internal workflows, 
supported by a stronger enterprise data and analytics 
ecosystem focused on data quality, real-time insights 
and scalable infrastructure.
As innovation accelerates, responsible adoption remains 
critical. The IT Strategy Committee and Information 
Systems Security Committee continue to strengthen 
oversight on AI governance, including data privacy, 
model risk, explainability, bias mitigation, cybersecurity, 
generative AI risks and adversarial threats.
Strong Governance, Risk & 
Compliance Guardrails
The Board, supported by Directors with diverse domain 
expertise and focused Committees, remains committed to 
responsible growth and the highest standards of corporate 
governance. As the operating environment becomes more 
complex, traditional risks such as credit, market, liquidity 
and operational risks are increasingly accompanied by 
emerging risks, including technology and cybersecurity, 
climate, model risk, money-mule activities, digital frauds 
and data protection challenges. Monitoring and mitigating 
these risks remains a key priority for the Risk Management 
Committee and the Board.
The Board maintains a zero-tolerance approach to 
governance lapses and accords the highest priority to a 
compliance-plus approach as a strategic imperative.  
It continues to define the Bank’s risk appetite, ensure strict 
regulatory adherence and embed accountability across the 
organisation through a three-lines-of-defence model, which 
is essential to building a ‘forever institution’.
In Closing
With such strong foundations in place, we await the 
Reserve Bank of India’s final approval for our transition to 
a Universal Bank. While our operating scope will certainly 
expand, our philosophy will remain unchanged: a retail-
focused, customer-centric and digital-first institution 
committed to long-term value creation.
I take this opportunity to extend my sincere gratitude to my 
fellow Board members for their guidance, our employees for 
their dedication and discipline, our customers for their trust, 
our regulators for their stewardship, and our shareholders 
and other stakeholders for their continued confidence in 
the momentous journey of the Bank.
As we look ahead, we remain confident that AU SFB 
will continue to strengthen its capabilities, deepen its 
relationships and build an institution that stands the test of 
time while remaining firmly anchored to its values.  
 
I complete my message with the profound words from 
Mahatma Gandhi that feel so relevant for our journey  
as a Forever Bank: 
Your beliefs become your thoughts.
Your thoughts become your words.
Your words become your actions.
Your actions become your habits.
Your habits become your values.
Your values become your destiny.
Warm regards,

Dear AU Bank Family,
Namaskar.
FY 2025-26 has been a defining year in AU SFB’s journey. 
On April 19, 2026, we completed nine years as a Bank, 
while also marking three decades since the founding of the 
institution. These milestones reflect not only the passage 
of time, but the strength of a vision that has steadily 
evolved from a vehicle finance company into one of India’s 
most admired financial institutions. The year was further 
distinguished by a landmark achievement—your Bank 
receiving the Reserve Bank of India’s in-principle approval 
to transition into a Universal Bank. This is a moment of 
immense significance, not only for AU SFB, but for every 
stakeholder who has been part of our journey.
The RBI’s in-principle approval is far more than a 
regulatory milestone. It is a recognition of the institution 
we have built with Purpose, Prudence and Patience 
over the last three decades. It reflects confidence in 
our business model, governance standards, financial 
resilience and our unwavering commitment to serving 
customers responsibly. Most importantly, it validates our 
belief that financial inclusion and sustainable growth are 
not competing objectives, but complementary goals that 
reinforce each other.
Banking is fundamentally a business of trust. 
Customers entrust us with their savings, their 
businesses, their aspirations and often a lifetime of 
hard work.
I have always believed in the above lines. Every decision 
we take must honour that trust. Products will evolve, 
technology will change and markets will fluctuate, but trust 
remains timeless.
To me, AU SFB has always been more than a Bank; it 
is a mission to build a more inclusive and enterprising 
India, one customer at a time and this milestone belongs 
as much to our customers and employees as it does to 
the institution. We mark this momentous occasion with 
gratitude, not simply for how far we have travelled, but also 
for the discipline and consistency that got us here, and that 
will carry us into our next chapter of growth. 
 
Growing the Right Way
FY 2025-26 was a year of disciplined execution against a 
backdrop of evolving market conditions. While our financial 
performance remained strong, our focus extends beyond 
annual results. We are investing in the franchise capabilities 
that will define AU SFB’s next decade of growth. Across our 
deposit franchise, asset distribution, technology platforms, 
leadership bench and governance infrastructure, we 
continue to invest heavily with a long-term perspective  
of preparing the institution for a larger scale and 
opportunities ahead.
Your Bank delivered a Profit After Tax of ₹2,641 Crore in 
FY 2025-26, with Return on Assets improving to 1.6% and 
Return on Equity at 14.2%, outcomes that reflect both the 
resilience of our franchise and the quality of our execution.
If there is one area that will shape the strength of AU 
SFB’s next phase, it is our deposit franchise. Building a

Dear Stakeholders,
At AU Small Finance Bank, our growth journey continues 
to be guided by a strong belief that sustainable banking 
is built on prudent risk management, customer-centricity, 
disciplined execution and long-term value creation.
Over the years, we have built a diversified and resilient 
lending franchise anchored in secured retail assets, 
granular portfolios and calibrated sectoral exposure. Our 
Wheels and Mortgage businesses continue to demonstrate 
structural strength, supported by deep customer 
understanding, collateral-backed underwriting, extensive 
distribution reach and proven collection capabilities. These 
businesses remain important pillars of stability, profitability 
and long-term franchise value.
In Commercial Banking, we continue to follow a focused 
sectoral approach centred on businesses where we 
possess strong underwriting expertise, ecosystem 
understanding and relationship depth. Our approach 
remains anchored on cash-flow assessment, risk-calibrated 
growth and granular exposure management, enabling us to 
support entrepreneurship while maintaining  
portfolio resilience.
The past year witnessed stress across select unsecured 
retail segments, including Microfinance, Credit Cards and 
Personal Loans. Encouragingly, we are now seeing signs 
of stabilisation and improving credit behaviour across 
these portfolios. With tighter underwriting, stronger 
risk segmentation, portfolio seasoning and improving 
macroeconomic conditions, we believe growth momentum 
is likely to strengthen progressively while remaining aligned 
with prudent risk management principles.
Technology and analytics are becoming increasingly 
central to our credit architecture. We are investing in 
AI-led Loan Origination Systems, automated decision 
engines, advanced underwriting models and early warning 
frameworks to improve scalability, consistency and 
customer experience. Beyond traditional scorecards, we 
are building capabilities that leverage data intelligence, 
behavioural insights, ecosystem data and AI-driven 
assessment frameworks to develop a sharper and more 
contextual understanding of customer risk.
Our objective is not merely faster credit delivery, but 
smarter and more responsible credit decisions. We believe 
the future of banking will belong to institutions that can 
combine technology-led agility with strong credit discipline 
and governance standards.
While the domestic economy continues to demonstrate 
remarkable resilience, we remain mindful of evolving global 
developments, particularly geopolitical uncertainties in 
West Asia. Any prolonged disruption could potentially 
impact energy prices, supply chains, and petrochemical-
linked industries, creating inflationary pressures across 
the economy. Such developments may have second-order 
and third-order effects on certain customer segments and 
portfolios through higher operating costs, pressure on 
disposable incomes, and moderation in business  
cash flows.
At AU SFB, we closely monitor these emerging risks 
through robust portfolio surveillance, stress-testing 
frameworks, and early warning mechanisms. Our diversified 
portfolio composition, strong secured asset franchise, and 
disciplined risk management approach position us well 
to navigate potential volatility. Importantly, based on the 
trends observed thus far, customer behaviour, portfolio 
performance, and asset quality indicators continue to 
remain stable and within our expected risk parameters. 
While we remain watchful and prepared for multiple 
scenarios, the operating environment today continues to 
support healthy credit growth and portfolio performance.
As India enters a new phase of economic expansion, the 
opportunity to deepen financial inclusion and support 
emerging Bharat remains immense. The consistency of our 
asset quality, the strength of our underwriting culture and 
the commitment of our teams continue to reinforce our 
confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead.
Together, we remain focused on building a trusted, resilient 
and differentiated banking franchise for all  
our stakeholders.

central to the Bank’s strategy during FY 2025-26. The Bank 
further strengthened the granularity of its deposit and asset

exceptional growth of 108% Y-o-Y. Micro Business

Materiality Assessment
Identification of Material Topics
At AU Small Finance Bank, we recognise that 
understanding what truly matters is fundamental to 
creating long-term value. Our materiality assessment is 
guided by the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Universal 
Standards, helping us remain aligned with global 
best practices while strengthening transparency and 
accountability.
During FY 2025-26, we undertook a comprehensive 
review to identify the economic, environmental, social, 
and governance topics most relevant to our business 
and stakeholders. This exercise was carried out in the 
context of an evolving banking landscape and growing 
expectations around responsible and sustainable 
practices.
Our approach is anchored in the GRI impact materiality 
lens, which considers both the impact of our operations 
on society and the environment, and the implications 
of these impacts on our long-term resilience. This 
perspective allows us to focus on areas that are 
meaningful not only to our stakeholders but also to the 
strength and sustainability of our business.
To build a well-rounded view, we engaged closely with 
both internal and external stakeholders across our value 
chain. These interactions helped us gather diverse 
perspectives and deepen our understanding of emerging 
priorities. Each topic was then assessed based on its 
strategic relevance, associated risks, and potential 
opportunities, ensuring that our priorities remain balanced 
and forward-looking.
The outcomes of this assessment have been published 
on our website (https://www.au.bank.in/sustainability-
disclosures), with all stakeholder inputs received up to 
the defined cut-off date incorporated into the Materiality 
Response Matrix. We continue to keep this process open, 
encouraging stakeholders to share their perspectives and 
contribute to future assessments.
Evaluation of Impact and 
Reprioritisation
We believe that a meaningful materiality process 
must remain dynamic and inclusive. To strengthen our 
assessment, we drew insights from ongoing interactions 
with our Board, key management personnel, employees, 
partners, and customers. This helped us evaluate both 
positive and negative impacts across our operations, value 
chain, financed activities, workforce, and communities.
By bringing these perspectives together, we are able to 
refine our priorities in a way that reflects both current 
realities and emerging trends, while supporting more 
informed decision-making.
Integration into Risk Management 
Framework
We have integrated our material topics into our risk 
management framework to better understand their 
implications for the business. Through this process, we 
identified a set of key opportunities alongside potential 
risks, informed by evolving impact trends and stakeholder 
expectations, including ESG priorities highlighted by 
investors.
This integration enables us to align sustainability 
considerations more closely with risk oversight and 
strategic planning, strengthening our ability to respond to 
change while pursuing responsible growth.
Materiality Matrix Sign-off
By prioritising topics based on their relative importance, we 
ensure that our actions remain focused on what matters 
most. This structured approach supports effective decision-
making, strengthens stakeholder trust, and reinforces our 
commitment to building a business that is both resilient and 
sustainable.

Build a Customer-centric

Customer centricity has been integral to AU SFB’s 
operating philosophy since inception and continues to be 
our foremost strategic priority. As we scale into a larger, 
more diversified and future-ready banking institution, our 
strategy remains anchored in a simple belief: sustainable 
growth is built on deep customer trust, consistent service 
delivery, and the ability to understand and serve evolving 
financial needs across every segment of society. For us, 
customer centricity is not a service initiative alone. It is the 
foundation of franchise building, influencing how we design 
products, build channels, deploy technology, manage  
risk, communicate with customers, and measure 
organisational performance.
We remain committed to delivering banking experiences 
that are accessible, seamless, transparent, fair and 
responsive. Customers span urban, semi-urban, and rural 
markets, salaried and self-employed individuals, small 
businesses, merchants, women entrepreneurs, farmers, 
micro-enterprises, and emerging affluent households. 
Each segment has distinct aspirations, financial behaviours 
and servicing needs. Our strategy is therefore to 
build a customer-centric ecosystem that allows us to 
serve customers with greater relevance, empathy and 
consistency across their financial journeys. We believe that 
the future of banking will belong to institutions that can 
combine scale with personalisation, digital convenience 
with human support, and innovation with responsibility.
A central pillar of this strategy is the creation of a 
comprehensive 360-degree view of the customer. 
We are investing in data analytics and technology 
capabilities that provide a deeper understanding of 
customer needs, preferences, behaviours, lifecycle events, 
and financial aspirations. This approach enables us to move 
beyond product-led engagement towards relationship-
led banking. A holistic view of the customer allows our 
teams to offer more relevant solutions, anticipate service 
needs, identify opportunities for responsible cross-
sell, and provide timely assistance. It also helps reduce 
fragmentation in customer engagement, ensuring that 
customers experience AU SFB as one unified Bank rather 
than a collection of products or channels.
Our customer-centric strategy is also focused on 
delivering a differentiated omnichannel experience. 
Customers today expect convenience, speed, and 
consistency, but they also value trust, advice, and 
assurance, particularly in important financial decisions. 
Our approach is therefore digital-first, but not digital-only. 
We integrate physical, assisted and digital channels so 
that customers can engage with us through the channel of 
their choice. Branches, banking outlets, relationship teams, 
contact centres, video banking, mobile platforms, and 
assisted digital channels all have an important role to play 
in delivering a seamless customer experience. The aim is 
to ensure that when a customer starts a journey digitally, 
seeks support through an assisted channel or completes a 
transaction at a branch, the experience remains consistent, 
convenient and reliable.
Innovation in products and solutions will remain an 
important driver of customer engagement. 
We will continue to design segment-focused offerings that 
address specific financial needs and deepen customer 
relationships. This includes solutions that support savings, 
deposits, payments, credit, business banking, insurance, 
wealth, and other financial requirements across the 
customer lifecycle. By tailoring offerings to customer 
segments and use cases, we seek to enhance relevance 
and improve outcomes. Our focus is not merely on 
acquiring customers, but on building enduring relationships 
by becoming a trusted financial partner across life stages, 
business cycles, and evolving aspirations.
End-to-end journey automation is another  
key priority. 
We are focused on simplifying onboarding, servicing, and 
closure processes to reduce customer effort and improve 
turnaround times. Automation across customer journeys 
will help eliminate avoidable friction, improve process 
consistency, and strengthen service delivery across 
channels. It will also enable faster resolution of service 
requests, better tracking of customer interactions, and 
improved accountability within the organisation. As we 
grow, such automation will be critical to maintaining service 
quality at scale while ensuring that our frontline teams can 
spend more time on meaningful customer engagement.
Technology, data and artificial intelligence will play  
a central role in the next phase of customer experience 
transformation. 
We are building an AI-enabled service model that can 
improve responsiveness, accuracy and consistency 
across customer touchpoints. Capabilities such as voice 
bots, virtual assistants, AI-driven complaint management, 
knowledge engines, and agent-assist tools can help us 
deliver faster and more informed support to customers. 
These tools can also help our employees serve customers 
better by providing relevant information, guiding resolution, 
and reducing dependency on manual processes. Our 
objective is to use technology to make banking simpler and 
more responsive, while ensuring that customers continue to 
experience care, transparency and accountability.
At the same time, we recognise that responsible use 
of technology is essential to preserving trust. As digital 
adoption expands and AI-led capabilities become more 
embedded in banking operations, customer protection, 
privacy, fairness, and transparency will remain central to 
our approach. Customer data must be used responsibly, 
with appropriate governance, security, and consent

frameworks. Our technology-led service transformation 
will therefore be guided by strong risk management,

Customer grievance redressal is a critical pillar of 
customer trust, governance and franchise building. 
We view every complaint as an opportunity to listen, learn, 
and improve. Our objective is to ensure that grievances 
are addressed fairly, transparently, and effectively, 
while making external escalation an exception rather 
than the norm. A strong redressal framework reinforces 
customer confidence  and provides valuable insight into 
service gaps, process issues, and emerging customer 
expectations. It also strengthens accountability across the 
organisation by ensuring that customer concerns are not 
treated as isolated events, but as signals for continuous 
improvement.
Our emphasis is increasingly shifting from complaint 
handling to complaint prevention. 
This requires disciplined root-cause analysis, proactive 
remediation, and continuous monitoring of grievance 
trends. By identifying recurring issues and addressing 
them at the source, we can improve customer experience 
structurally rather than only resolving concerns after they 
arise. This approach will be supported by data-driven 
insights, journey mapping, feedback loops, and stronger 
ownership across business, operations, technology, 
and service teams. Embedding customer-centric 
accountability across the organisation will be essential to 
building a consistently high-quality service culture.
To institutionalise this strategy, we are strengthening 
our customer excellence framework around measurable 
outcomes. 
Key indicators such as Net Promoter Score, Customer 
Satisfaction Score, First Contact Resolution, complaint 
ratios, digital adoption, and service quality metrics will help 
us measure progress more objectively. These metrics will 
enable us to track customer experience across journeys, 
channels, segments, identify improvement areas, and 
align teams around a common service agenda. A strong 
measurement framework is important because customer 
centricity must be managed with the same discipline as 
growth, productivity, risk, and profitability.
Building a customer-centric franchise is therefore our 
topmost strategic priority because it directly supports 
every dimension of long-term value creation. It strengthens 
trust, improves retention, deepens relationships, supports 
responsible growth, and enhances the quality of the 
franchise. As we continue to grow, our ability to remain 
close to customers, understand their needs, and respond 
with speed and fairness will define the strength of our 
institution.
Our ambition is to build a Bank that customers choose not 
only for products, but for confidence, convenience and 
care. By combining customer insight, omnichannel reach, 
responsible innovation, proactive service, and strong 
governance, we aim to create a differentiated banking 
experience that is simple, inclusive, and future-ready. 
This customer-first mindset will continue to guide our 
transformation journey and support our aspiration to build 
an enduring institution that serves generations with trust, 
transparency and responsibility.

four mutually reinforcing levers: disciplined, segment-led 
growth; deepened distribution; the structural advantages 
of a universal banking license; and technology and AI-led 
enablement across the value chain. Together, these levers 
are designed to deliver growth that is calibrated, granular, 
and resilient through cycles.

Universal Banking and  
ease of business
We expect our potential transition to a universal Bank to 
be a structural step-change, rather than a mere change in 
nomenclature. It expands our addressable opportunity and 
unlocks several levers that can directly support our loan 
portfolio growth:
Technology and  
AI-led enablement
Technology and AI are increasingly becoming the 
operating layer through which AU SFB intends to 
scale growth, strengthen distribution and manage the 
complexity associated with its potential transition to a 
Universal Bank. During FY 2025-26, the Bank accelerated 
its investments in Agentic AI with a clear focus on 
enhancing productivity, improving customer experience 
and creating sustainable operating leverage.

»
Lower Priority Sector Lending (PSL) 
commitment:
As per regulatory norms, Small Finance Banks 
are currently required to allocate 60% of their 
Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to Priority 
Sector Lending (PSL) with focus on farmer 
financing, agriculture ecosystem, housing, 
education and MSME etc. This PSL requirement 
reduces meaningfully to 40% of ANBC upon 
our transition to a universal bank. This will 
reduce our operating intensity around PSL 
classification, documentation, and monitoring, 
allowing our underwriting and business teams 
to deploy bandwidth more productively towards 
growing the business. While our underlying 
customer segment and business segments are 
not expected to change much, focus will shift 
from more compliance driven lending to a more 
opportunity and credit driven decision making.
	
»
Removal of ticket-size restrictions:
In compliance with Reserve Bank of India (RBI) 
guidelines applicable to Small Finance Banks, we 
deploy a minimum of 50% of our loan portfolio 
in ticket sizes of up to ₹25 Lakh. On transition to 
a universal bank, while we will continue to cater 
to the small ticket size loans, the removal of this 
regulatory constraint will enable us to participate 
more fully in larger-ticket opportunities across 
Mortgages, Commercial Banking, and Corporate 
Relationships, areas where our current 
participation has been shaped by regulatory 
ceilings rather than a lack of capability.
	
»
Enhanced brand and counterparty acceptance: 
Once the transition to a universal Bank is 
complete, it is expected to improve our 
counterparty comfort, institutional credibility, 
and eligibility for government, public-sector, and 
large-corporate relationships. Over time, this 
can support both sides of our balance sheet-
improving our ability to source quality assets as 
well as deepening our liability relationships.
Importantly, this transition arrives after our core 
foundations have already been built. Our governance 
architecture, leadership depth, a unified core banking 
platform (post the erstwhile Fincare integration), and 
a distribution network that has nearly doubled over 
two years, are all firmly in place. The universal banking 
milestone therefore becomes an accelerator of our already-
strengthened franchise, rather than the starting point for 
capability-building.
Collectively, these investments are helping build a more 
intelligent and scalable operating model that improves 
productivity, enhances customer experience and supports 
higher business volumes and broader product offerings, 
while maintaining cost discipline and risk controls.

Strong Governance and 
Risk Management
Governance as a strategic 
foundation
Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) remains a critical 
cornerstone of the Bank given its role as a custodian of 
public deposits, supported by a well-established and 
institutionalised framework that upholds high standards 
of governance, transparency, and accountability. Strong 
governance and disciplined risk management provide the 
stability and confidence required to scale sustainably. 
As we progress towards becoming a universal banking 
franchise, our governance and risk management framework 
has been deliberately strengthened to keep pace with the 
increasing scale, complexity and responsibility of  
the institution.
The Reserve Bank of India’s in-principle approval for our 
transition to a Universal Bank in August 2025 is more than 
a regulatory milestone; it reflects the trust and confidence 
the Bank has built through years of consistent, transparent 
and accountable conduct.
Independence of Board and  
control functions
The governance framework is further strengthened by a 
balanced and diversified Board with a strong independent 
presence, enabling effective oversight, objective decision-
making, and prudent risk stewardship. Importantly, 
governance, risk, compliance, and audit functions operate 
as independent oversight mechanisms and are not driven 
by business targets, thereby minimising potential conflicts 
of interest and ensuring unbiased risk assessment and 
regulatory compliance.
Independence extends beyond the Board to the control 
functions that sit beneath it. Risk, Compliance and 
Internal Audit operate independent of business lines 
each with clearly defined mandates, direct access to 
Board committees, and the authority to escalate without 
interference. The Head of Internal Audit reports directly to 
the Audit Committee, ensuring that assurance is objective 
and autonomous. Similarly, Chief Risk Officer (CRO) reports 
to the Risk Management Committee of the Board.
The Bank follows a well-defined Three Lines of Defence 
framework comprising business and control functions as 
the first line, independent Risk and Compliance functions 
as the second line, and Internal Audit as the third line, 
ensuring robust internal controls and multiple layers of 
oversight. Dedicated functions across Risk, Compliance, 
Internal Audit, Secretarial, and Vigilance continuously 
strengthen governance standards through comprehensive 
risk management, policy oversight, and control monitoring. 
The Bank will continue to enhance its enterprise-wide 
risk assessment framework, including credit, operational, 
market, liquidity, conduct, and emerging risks, supported by 
technology-enabled monitoring and advanced analytics.
	
»
Credit governance
Sound credit governance remains central to our 
credit risk management philosophy. The Credit Risk 
Committee, supported by clearly defined risk appetite 
frameworks and underwriting standards, oversees 
credit risk across our lending portfolio. Enhancing our 
credit decisioning capabilities through the adoption 
of AI-first platforms, enabling more consistent, data-
driven credit assessments and early risk detection 
remain key focus areas for the Bank.
Our ICAAP and periodic stress-testing exercises ensure 
that capital buffers remain adequate under adverse 
scenarios, and that credit risk concentrations are 
monitored proactively. The outcome of these processes 
are reported regularly to the Risk Management 
Committee and the Board.
	
»
Fraud prevention and vigilance
We maintain a structured and multi-layered approach to 
fraud prevention and vigilance. The Special Committee 
of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of Cases 
provides Board-level oversight of fraud risk, reviewing 
root-cause analyses, monitoring recovery positions, 
and ensuring that systemic weaknesses are addressed 
through strengthened controls.
The Whistle Blower and Vigil Mechanism provide 
a formal channel for employees, customers, and 
stakeholders to report concerns with direct access to 
the Audit Committee Chairperson for escalation.  
No legitimate concern is left without a pathway  
to resolution.
	
»
Expanding risk management to emerging areas
Expanding our Enterprise Risk Management framework 
to address emerging risk categories alongside 
traditional financial risks remains a key priority. A 
partnership with the International Finance Corporation 
(IFC) to integrate climate risk into core banking strategy 
is a significant project which will help embedding 
physical and transition risk considerations into lending 
decisions and portfolio management.

Usage of data analytics
Data analytics now sits at the core of how AU SFB acquires 
customers, underwrites credit and manages risk across 
its lending businesses. We have built a growing library 
of in-house models, including classification models that 
help segment customers and assess eligibility, application

business-rules engine, credit policy is applied consistently

decisions with less manual intervention.

decisioning is being extended into Vehicle Finance and 
Commercial Banking portfolios. As more data accrues,

changes in risk earlier and respond more precisely.

Responsible innovation and governance
As artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded 
in banking, sound governance becomes more important, 
not less. Our approach rests on five core principles - ethics, 
transparency, accountability, security and compliance. 
Human judgement remains central to every critical decision, 
and AI models are subject to validation, monitoring and 
periodic review.
Protecting customers from financial crime is a central part 
of this responsibility. We currently have eight scorecards 
live across Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and mule-account 
monitoring, and more than 60% of transaction-monitoring 
alerts are now reviewed and resolved through automated 
decisioning within defined risk thresholds. Solutions  
such as Amlytics and MuleHunter.ai strengthen 
surveillance, while AI-powered fraud engines continue 
to improve monitoring accuracy, alert prioritisation and 
investigative effectiveness.

Cyber resilience remains a board-level priority. During the

India’s economic momentum is ushering in a new phase 
of sustained credit expansion, but one that is unfolding 
in a far more complex and rapidly evolving environment 
than seen before. Rising borrower leverage, the 
growing influence of digital lending, tighter regulatory 
expectations, frequent macroeconomic and geopolitical 
disruptions are collectively reshaping the risk landscape.
At AU Small Finance Bank (AU SFB), we recognise that 
the focus cannot simply be on growing the balance sheet, 
but on scaling in a manner that preserves asset quality 
and delivers predictable, risk-adjusted returns. This belief 
forms the foundation of our credit governance approach, 
where precision underwriting, disciplined risk alignment, 
and forward-looking monitoring are embedded at every 
stage of the credit lifecycle. 
Recognising this shift, we aligned the entire credit 
governance function under one umbrella and created the 
post of Chief Credit Officer (CCO) of the Bank. Under the 
CCO department, we have consolidated underwriting, 
portfolio monitoring, asset quality, security enforcement, 
legal and collection architectures as well as credit policy. 
Our effort has been to build a credit model that is both 
sustainable and scalable. Sustainability is ensuring that 
portfolio behaviour remains stable across cycles, credit 
costs are predictable, and underwriting practices are fully 
aligned with regulatory and audit expectations. A key shift 
we have made is moving from a purely deal-level lens to a 
portfolio-centric view of risk, allowing us to assess not just 
individual exposures but also concentrations, correlations, 
and systemic vulnerabilities. At the same time, by being 
consistent across geographies and segments and 
adaptable to new products, scalability is being driven 
through data-led and digitally enabled decision-making.

approach to underwriting and adopting a more granular,

risk exposures through detailed evaluation. Expanding STP, 
particularly in retail portfolios, is improving turnaround times 
and cost efficiency while maintaining consistency. We are 
also strengthening pre-approved and pre-qualified funnels, 
which help improve conversion and reduce acquisition and 
underwriting costs.
Technology-Led Credit Decision: Integrating rules, 
scorecards, analytics and segmented underwriting for 
faster, more consistent credit decisions.
Recognising that risk evolves continuously, we are 
strengthening our early warning and monitoring capabilities 
using data and analytics, tracking real-time indicators 
such as banking behaviour changes, GST movements, 
credit bureau triggers, and EMI repayment patterns. These 
are linked to structured action frameworks that enable 
timely interventions, including customer engagement, limit 
recalibration, and targeted collections. In parallel, we are 
enhancing our focus on portfolio-level governance. Through 
internal monitoring frameworks, we track key indicators 
such as vintage performance, delinquency flow rates across 
buckets, segment-wise stress build-up, and geographic 
concentrations. This provides a forward-looking view of 
portfolio health and enables dynamic decision-making, 
including tightening credit filters or recalibrating exposures 
in segments where early signs of stress emerge.
Real-Time Risk Monitoring: Tracking behavioural, 
GST, bureau and repayment indicators to enable 
proactive portfolio management.
Moreover, we believe that credit culture is equally critical. 
We place strong emphasis on embedding risk ownership 
within business teams, supported by maker-checker 
discipline and clear communication of risk appetite. 
Decision-making is encouraged to be balanced and 
prudent, including the ability to decline opportunities that 
do not meet risk standards. This is reinforced through 
aligned performance metrics, where growth is evaluated 
alongside portfolio quality, early delinquency indicators, 
slippages, and credit costs, ensuring that accountability is 
built across the credit lifecycle. 
 
The key principle guiding our approach is the need 
to balance credit cost with the cost of doing credit. 
Excessively conservative underwriting can result in missed 
opportunities and lower growth, while overly complex 
processes can increase operating costs and reduce 
efficiency. Our focus is on optimising the total cost of risk, 
which includes credit cost, origination cost, collection cost, 
and opportunity cost.

Scalable Growth Through Cross-Sell and 
Digital Acquisition
Cross-selling to our existing customer base (ETB)
and unlocking the full potential of our lead ecosystem 
represents one of the most capital-efficient growth levers 
at our disposal. With over 1.2 Crore customers across 
our deposit, asset and digital franchises, the opportunity 
to deepen relationships through additional products and 
services is both significant and largely untapped. We have 
adopted a resilient and focused approach on building a 
comprehensive, technology-enabled Cross-sell, Up-sell 
and Digital lead acquisition framework that brings together 
co-origination, referral and external lead streams of NTB 
customers into a single, analytics and AI-driven engine.
Building a scalable cross-sell and 
digital lead acquisition engine
Cross-sell and digital lead acquisition architecture 
framework is designed around three complementary 
opportunity pools: cross-sell, up-sell and digital lead 
acquisition, each supported by metadata, analytics and 
technology-led execution.
To support this framework of cross-sell and digital lead 
acquisition, we are building a centralised lead management 
and routing architecture. Leads from various sources are 
aggregated on a central data platform, qualified through 
analytics-based propensity models and scorecards and 
routed based on internal and external customer, lead 
quality, urgency and customer context.
	
»
Cross-sell opportunities are identified at the point of 
co-origination, enabling relevant product discovery 
when customer engagement is at its highest. These 
journeys are being embedded across our retail loan 
systems and liability platforms, allowing customers 
to receive a more holistic view of our offerings and 
enabling referrals across core journeys. 
Our lead management application for the sales  
team serves as the primary execution layer for self-
sourcing, cross-sell and lead assignment. Relationship 
managers can receive, manage and action leads 
through the platform, connect with customers directly 
from the interface and update customer interactions 
and dispositions. 
	
»
Up-sell focuses on deepening existing relationships 
within the same product vertical, such as encouraging 
savings account customers to open fixed deposits or 
offering enhanced loan eligibility to existing borrowers. 
Integration with Account Aggregator and other data 
sources provides real-time financial insights, helping us 
identify more relevant and timelier up-sell triggers for 
each customer.
	
»
Digital Lead Acquisition consolidates a wider 
funnel of externally sourced, referral-based and 
internally generated opportunities for NTB customers. 
Consolidation of all lead sources into a single platform 
allows us to monitor the engagement with each source 
in terms of lead flow and business conversion.

The Reserve Bank of India’s in-principle approval for AU 
SFB’s transition to a Universal Bank on August 7, 2025 
marked a defining milestone in our journey, reflecting nearly 
three decades of disciplined institution building. The Bank 
became the first Small Finance Bank in India to receive an 
in-principle Universal Banking license.  
 
The RBI recognised the Bank’s satisfactory track record 
and fulfilment of the eligibility criteria under the voluntary 
transition framework issued in April 2024. Pursuant to the 
Bank’s request, RBI replaced the requirement relating to 
the establishment of a Non-Operative Financial Holding 
Company (NOFHC). Under the revised condition, the 
requirement would arise only if the Bank or its promoter 
group seeks to establish a group entity in the future, 
thereby streamlining the transition pathway. In March 
2026, the Bank submitted its final license application to the 
RBI, marking another significant step towards becoming a 
Universal Bank.
Progressing Towards Universal 
Banking
Expanding our opportunity
The potential transition to a Universal Bank significantly 
expands our strategic canvas. It broadens our addressable 
market, enhances operating flexibility and enables us to 
participate more comprehensively across our customers’ 
financial journeys. This creates opportunities to serve a 
wider spectrum of customer segments - including salaried 
professionals, affluent households, senior citizens, NRIs and 
larger commercial enterprises through an expanded suite 
of banking, payments, treasury, wealth management and 
transaction banking solutions.
The transition will remove several regulatory 
requirements associated with the Small Finance 
Bank framework, providing greater flexibility in 
portfolio construction, liability mobilisation and 
capital allocation, while enabling deeper and  
longer-lasting customer relationships. 
Strengthening  
long-term foundations
Beyond expanding business opportunities, universal 
banking license will enhance the structural 
strengths of the franchise. A broader deposit-
gathering capability, increased participation in 
government and institutional banking opportunities, 
wider market acceptance and greater refinancing 
flexibility collectively improve the resilience, 
diversification and scalability of the Bank.
The transition will also create additional avenues to 
drive operating leverage through greater flexibility 
across securitisation, co-lending and other  
strategic initiatives.
Importantly, we enter this phase from a position 
of strength. Over the years, we have consistently 
invested in technology, governance, risk 
management and operational capabilities aligned 
with Universal Banking standards. This transition will 
enable us to unlock the full potential of capabilities 
that have already been built and tested at scale.

The challenge
A merchant in a busy Rajasthan market was hesitant 
to adopt digital payments because he could not 
independently verify SMS confirmations. It was 
not distrust of technology that held him back. He 
simply could not read the SMS alerts that confirmed 
a payment had come through. Every digital 
transaction ended in a moment of uncertainty he 
had no way to resolve, and so he stayed with cash.
The solution
We installed an AU QR Sound Box at his shop. The 
audio confirmation removed the need to interpret 
SMS alerts and reduced uncertainty at the point of 
payment.
The impact
The instant audio confirmation improved the 
merchant's confidence in digital transactions and 
encouraged regular usage. Today, the merchant 
is active within the formal digital payments 
ecosystem, with a transaction record that has 
improved his access to credit. It allowed him to 
expand his stock, and helped him grow his shop 
in ways he could not have imagined before. This 
illustrates how accessible technology can convert 
trust into measurable business outcomes.

At AU SFB, green finance sits at the heart of our 
sustainable finance strategy. We believe that financial 
products can do much more than generate returns. They 
can regenerate ecosystems, reduce emissions, and 
broaden access to a cleaner economy. Through these 
lending flows and deposit-linked deployments, the Bank 
translates climate ambition into measurable financial 
action: not through mere statements, but through lending 
flows and deposit funds.
Planet First –  
AU Green Fixed Deposit
Launched in line with the RBI’s Green Deposit Guidelines, 
Planet First – AU Green Fixed Deposit enables customers 
to align their savings with environmentally responsible 
projects, contributing to environmental conservation while 
earning assured returns. The product is supported by 
transparent reporting on the deployment of funds and the 
outcomes achieved through green investments.
Governed by a Board-approved Green Deposit Policy and 
aligned with RBI guidelines, the programme integrates 
ESG considerations into lending practices and is 
supported by independent third-party validation to ensure 
credibility and accountability.
Sustainable Finance
As of March 31, 2026, the programme has mobilised 
over ₹2,950 Crore via 24,520 accounts. The funds flow 
exclusively into three categories:
Renewable energy — solar and agri-renewable projects, 
including under PM-KUSUM, reducing diesel dependence 
for farmers and expanding clean generation capacity in line 
with India’s 500 GW target by 2030.
Clean transportation — specialised EV loans for two-
wheelers, passenger vehicles, and commercial vehicles, 
supporting gender-inclusive access to clean mobility.
Green buildings — projects certified under ASSOCHAM 
(GEM 4), IGBC (Gold), and comparable standards.
ESG risk and  
climate risk integration
Managing ESG risks is integral to building a resilient 
and responsible banking system. We have initiated 
the integration of ESG considerations into our credit 
assessment and decision-making processes through 
structured evaluation frameworks. We assess green 
projects for environmental and social compliance to 
evaluate potential risks and impacts, enabling us to make 
more informed and responsible lending decisions.
During FY 2025-26, AU SFB became the first Indian Bank to 
partner with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) on 
Climate Risk Advisory. This enables the Bank to incorporate 
physical risks, such as flooding, heat stress and water 
scarcity, as well as transition risks, including policy shifts, 
technology disruption and asset stranding, into lending and 
risk processes.

Transparent disclosure is central to accountability. As 
climate risk becomes increasingly material to financial 
decision-making, robust reporting enables stakeholders to 
assess the progress and credibility of our commitments.
ESG governance
Our ESG disclosures are aligned with globally recognised 
frameworks, including BRSR and GRI, while ensuring 
compliance with SEBI’s reporting guidelines and adhering 
to the principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible 
Business Conduct (NGRBC). The Bank has established a 
robust three-tier governance structure that embeds ESG 
principles across strategy, operations, and reporting, with 
strong Board oversight and organisation-wide integration. 
Governance is operationalised through strategic decision-
making, regular performance monitoring by the Committee, 
and comprehensive BRSR disclosures backed by third-
party assurance. This approach strengthens transparency, 
credibility, and resilience, enabling effective tracking of 
climate and social impact while reinforcing stakeholder 
trust and supporting India’s sustainable development 
agenda and long-term stakeholder value creation.
Sustainability ratings
ESG ratings provide an external benchmark of the Bank’s 
sustainability performance, enabling stakeholders to 
assess progress against peer practices, disclosure 
standards and evolving expectations. Across key 
platforms, AU SFB holds an S&P Global (CSA) score of 47, 
a Sustainalytics score of 16.6 (Low Risk), an NSE score of 
73 (Strong) and an ESG Risk Assessments & Insights score 
of 69 (Strong). For the Bank, these ratings represent a 
reference point for continuous improvement, with ongoing 
focus on strengthening performance, disclosures and 
governance standards.
Sustainability 
Reporting
As a financial institution, we recognise that environmental 
sustainability requires active investment in the ecological 
health of the communities and geographies we serve. The 
communities where we operate, many of them rural, water-
stressed, or ecologically vulnerable, bear a disproportionate 
share of climate risk despite having a comparatively 
lower direct contribution to climate-related impacts. Our 
responsibility, therefore, extends beyond responsible 
lending and cleaner operations to direct stewardship: 
conserving water bodies, restoring green cover, and 
building environmental awareness at the grassroots. 
When communities are ecologically resilient, they are also 
economically resilient, and that connection between natural 
capital and human progress is one we take seriously in 
everything we do.
Freshwater is perhaps the most critical natural capital asset 
in the Indian context. As part of World Water Day initiatives 
during FY 2025-26, the Bank supported the restoration 
of Medavakkam Lake and Pazhathotta Pond in Chennai, 
contributing to urban water body conservation, biodiversity, 
groundwater recharge, and community resilience in 
ecologically stressed environments.
Plantation drives and Green Lit Fest
Nationwide plantation campaigns spanning a full month 
were conducted during FY 2025-26, aligned with the 
Government’s ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam 2.0’ initiative and 
Van Mahotsava, contributing to carbon sequestration and 
biodiversity support across our footprint. Our support for 
the Green Lit Fest extended the Bank’s environmental voice 
beyond operations, creating a platform for sustainability 
education, storytelling, and stakeholder engagement. These 
initiatives create platforms for sustainability education, 
stakeholder engagement and environmental awareness.
By expanding green finance, improving operational 
efficiency, investing in ecological resilience and 
strengthening sustainability disclosures, we are building an 
institution whose long-term prosperity is aligned with the 
health of the environment in which it operates.

Key Risks and Mitigation
We have established a strong risk culture and risk governance framework to enable risk assessment, identification, 
measurement, mitigation and reporting of risks within the Bank.
Key risks and their mitigation framework are as follows:
Credit risk management
Credit risk refers to the potential 
loss arising from a borrower’s or 
counterparty’s failure to meet their 
contractual obligations, including 
repayments, settlements, or other 
financial commitments.
Mitigation
The Credit Risk unit is responsible for assessing and monitoring credit risk via 
setting up thresholds, risk limits and closely tracking asset quality. It conducts 
periodic portfolio reviews, aligned with our evolving risk appetite and business 
plans. Oversight extends to credit strategy, underwriting and risk frameworks 
like early warning systems, portfolio triggers, risk classifications and high-value 
exposure monitoring. By adopting a forward-looking approach and leveraging 
data analytics, the Credit Risk function ensures resilience in a dynamic 
economic and regulatory environment, supporting our long-term sustainability.
We follow a robust credit risk architecture with defined policies and systems 
for both retail and commercial lending. While commercial loans are managed 
on a standalone basis as well as on portfolio basis, retail lending, due to its 
granularity, is largely managed on a portfolio basis. Emphasis is placed on 
diversification, prudent credit approvals, post-disbursement monitoring and 
corrective actions.
The Credit Risk Management Committee (CRMC) monitors large exposures, 
asset quality, and portfolio concentration. The CRMC reviews portfolio trends, 
sector-level exposures, and emerging stress indicators, ensuring timely and 
calibrated risk mitigation. Its findings are submitted to the Board-level Risk 
Management Committee every quarter.
Operational risk management
Operational risk, as defined by 
the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), 
refers to the risk of loss arising 
from inadequate or failed internal 
processes, people, systems, or 
external events. It includes legal 
risk but excludes strategic and 
reputational risks.
Mitigation
We manage operational risk through a Board-approved Operational Risk 
Management Policy supported by a robust framework covering governance, 
processes, and controls across all business verticals. The framework follows 
the three lines of defence model:
1.	 First Line: Business units, support functions, and operations
2.	 Second Line: Independent Operational Risk Management Department 
(ORMD)
3.	 Third Line: Internal Audit
The ORMD is responsible for implementing the operational risk framework 
across the Bank. Oversight is provided by the ORMC, which monitors 
effectiveness, reviews key risk issues, and recommends mitigation measures. 
The ORMC reports to the RMC, ensuring effective Board-level supervision and 
governance. 
Fraud risk management
Fraud risks are managed through a dedicated Fraud Control Unit (FCU) 
operating under a Board-approved Fraud Risk Management Policy. The FCU is 
responsible for identification, investigation, and containment of fraud incidents 
across the Bank. Oversight of significant fraud cases is provided by the Special 
Committee of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of Cases of Fraud 
(SCBMF), which reviews root cause analyses and monitors the implementation 
of corrective and preventive actions.
We continuously strengthen our systems and monitoring capabilities through 
real-time transaction surveillance, enhanced internal controls, and increased

staff vigilance. Regular training and awareness programmes are conducted 
to sensitise employees to emerging fraud risks and reinforce a culture of 
accountability and prevention. 
Outsourcing risk management
We follow comprehensive IT and Financial Services Outsourcing Policies 
aligned with RBI guidelines. While the Board retains ultimate responsibility for 
outsourcing arrangements, operational oversight is delegated to the Committee 
for Outsourcing of IT and Financial Services, which reports to the RMC. The 
framework ensures structured due diligence, risk assessment, monitoring, and 
governance of all outsourced activities.
Business continuity management
We have a well-defined Business Continuity Management (BCM) framework, 
which is periodically reviewed to remain aligned with regulatory requirements 
and evolving risk scenarios. The framework includes dedicated Disaster 
Recovery sites, periodic business continuity drills, and emergency response 
plans covering IT disruptions and pandemic scenarios. Learnings from 
simulations and drills are used to continuously strengthen resilience and ensure 
continuity of critical operations during disruptions.
Digital risk mitigation
With the rapid expansion of digital channels, we have reinforced our monitoring 
and control framework across all platforms. Enhanced system controls, 
continuous risk assessments, and advanced surveillance mechanisms ensure a 
secure and seamless customer experience while aligning with our digital growth 
strategy.
Market risk, liquidity and asset liability management
Market risk arises from adverse 
movements in interest rates, 
foreign exchange rates and market 
prices impacting the Bank’s trading 
and investment activities, including 
customer-driven and proprietary 
transactions. With the expansion 
of treasury activities and derivative 
transactions, the risk profile 
continues to evolve in line with 
market developments and business 
requirements. Liquidity risk arises 
from the inability to meet cash flow 
and collateral obligations, both 
expected and unexpected, without 
adversely impacting the Bank’s 
financial position. Market risk and 
liquidity risk remain key areas of 
focus under the Bank’s balance 
sheet management framework.
Mitigation
Market and liquidity risks are managed through a comprehensive framework 
comprising Board-approved policies, risk limits, regulatory guidelines, and 
robust monitoring mechanisms. Risk measurement methodologies, analytical 
tools and periodic stress testing are employed for continuous assessment 
of exposures across investment portfolios, foreign exchange positions, and 
derivative transactions. The framework also includes regular monitoring of 
liquidity positions, funding concentrations, and maturity profiles to ensure 
adequate liquidity and balance sheet resilience under both normal and 
stressed conditions. The ALCO provides oversight on market, liquidity, foreign 
exchange, and interest rate risks through periodic review of risk exposures, 
market developments, and compliance with internal and regulatory thresholds. 
The overall risk management approach remains aligned with our risk appetite 
and strategic objectives while supporting prudent balance sheet and treasury 
management practices.
Information and cybersecurity management
As we advance our digital journey 
to enhance customer experience 
and operational efficiency, we 
remain vigilant against cyber risks. 
Threats such as malware, phishing, 
denial-of-service attacks and data 
breaches pose potential risks to 
systems, services and sensitive 
information. 
Mitigation
We have a robust information and cybersecurity framework to safeguard our 
IT infrastructure and data assets. Risks are identified, assessed, mitigated 
and monitored through dedicated governance structures, including Board 
and management-level committees. The Chief Information Security Officer 
(CISO), reporting to the MD & CEO, oversees our information security posture, 
supported by a 24x7 Cyber Security Operations Centre (C-SOC) for real-time 
threat monitoring.

The world economy, which was broadly resilient in 2025, is facing renewed headwinds, primarily due to geopolitical 
tensions, particularly the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. As a baseline scenario, the IMF’s April 2026 World Economic 
Outlook has projected global growth at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027, which is below the long-term historical average 
growth of 3.7%. However, in a more adverse scenario involving prolonged conflict, growth could fall to approximately 2.5%. 
In a severe scenario with significant disruption to global energy supplies or trade routes, growth could even drop to 2%, 
approaching recessionary conditions.
Global Economy on Edge
Inflation has re-emerged as a key concern, with global 
inflation projected to rise to about 4.4% in 2026 before 
moderating to around 3.7% in 2027. The uptick in inflation is 
largely attributed to higher energy prices and supply chain 
disruptions, especially those affecting critical trade routes. 
This has complicated the task of central banks, which 
now face an intense trade-off between maintaining tight 
monetary policy to control inflation and easing policy rates 
to support weakening growth.
As regards the growth outlook, risks are skewed to 
the downside. Key risks include further escalation of 
geopolitical tensions, persistently high oil prices, increasing 
trade fragmentation and protectionist measures, tightening 
global financial conditions, and high levels of public debt 
that limit fiscal space. There are some upside possibilities, 
such as stronger-than-expected gains from artificial 
intelligence or a faster easing of geopolitical tensions. 
Signing of MoU between the US and Iran for a ceasefire 
is considered to be a positive development, which is 
expected to normalise crude oil prices to the pre-war level 
if sanctions are removed against Iran on an enduring basis.
From a policy perspective, maintaining a credible monetary 
policy to anchor inflation expectations, even as growth 
slows, assumes importance. Globally, there is also a need 
to rebuild fiscal buffers, given elevated debt levels, and 
strengthen international cooperation to address shared 
challenges such as trade disruptions and energy security. 
Structural reforms aimed at boosting productivity, including 
through digitalisation and innovation, are also critical for 
medium-term growth.

to be particularly vulnerable due to their dependence on

flows. Within this group, India stands out, with growth

domestic demand and robust services exports, making it 
the fastest-growing major economy.
Broadly, the global economy is navigating a fragile phase 
marked by slowing growth, persistent inflation pressures, 
and elevated uncertainty. Geopolitical developments have 
become the dominant influence on the economic outlook, 
and the balance of risks remains tilted to the downside, 
requiring cautious and coordinated policy responses.

India’s macroeconomic performance in FY 2025-26 
remained robust. According to the provisional estimates 
by the NSO, India’s real GDP growth was 7.7% in FY 
2025-26, supported by strong domestic demand, resilient 
activity in the services sector, and sustained public capital 
expenditure. The economy demonstrated resilience despite 
global headwinds such as elevated global uncertainties, 
geopolitical tensions, reciprocal tariffs by the US, and 
commodity price volatility.
Private consumption showed steady improvement during 
the year, aided by easing inflation, rising rural incomes, 
and stable urban demand. Government capital expenditure 
continued to play a critical role in sustaining growth 
momentum, particularly through infrastructure development 
in transport, logistics, and energy sectors. Investment 
activity remained mixed, with public investment strong 
while private corporate investment showed gradual but 
uneven recovery, reflecting cautious business sentiment 
amid global uncertainties.
Inflation dynamics improved in FY 2025-26, with headline 
CPI inflation moderating to 2.1% compared to 4.6% in the 
previous year, mainly due to deflation in food prices in 
Q2 and Q3 of FY 2025-26. Core inflation showed signs of 
stickiness due to metal prices. The underlying inflation was 
weak as core inflation without gold and silver prices was 
extremely benign at 2.1%. The RBI maintained a neutral 
monetary policy stance since June 2025.
On the external front, India’s position remained manageable. 
While merchandise trade balance faced headwinds from 
the US tariff, higher crude oil prices, weak global demand 
and supply disruptions, services exports, especially in 
IT and business services, and remittances continued to 
provide strong support to the external current account. The 
Current Account Deficit (CAD) remained comfortable at 
0.6% of GDP in FY 2025-26 aided by resilient remittances 
and IT-enabled services. As capital flows were insufficient 
to finance the CAD, the exchange rate was under pressure, 
particularly towards the end of the year. Foreign exchange 
reserves remained comfortable, providing an adequate 
buffer against external shocks.
Fiscal policy continued to focus on consolidation while 
supporting growth. The central government adhered to its 
medium-term fiscal consolidation path, reducing the fiscal 
deficit gradually while maintaining high-quality expenditure, 
particularly on infrastructure. Tax revenues performed 
well, supported by strong economic activity and improved 
compliance, while subsidy burdens remained contained 
despite volatility in global commodity prices.
