Customer centricity has been integral to AU SFB’s 
operating philosophy since inception and continues to be 
our foremost strategic priority. As we scale into a larger, 
more diversified and future-ready banking institution, our 
strategy remains anchored in a simple belief: sustainable 
growth is built on deep customer trust, consistent service 
delivery, and the ability to understand and serve evolving 
financial needs across every segment of society. For us, 
customer centricity is not a service initiative alone. It is the 
foundation of franchise building, influencing how we design 
products, build channels, deploy technology, manage  
risk, communicate with customers, and measure 
organisational performance.
We remain committed to delivering banking experiences 
that are accessible, seamless, transparent, fair and 
responsive. Customers span urban, semi-urban, and rural 
markets, salaried and self-employed individuals, small 
businesses, merchants, women entrepreneurs, farmers, 
micro-enterprises, and emerging affluent households. 
Each segment has distinct aspirations, financial behaviours 
and servicing needs. O

ur strategy is therefore to 
build a customer-centric ecosystem that allows us to 
serve customers with greater relevance, empathy and 
consistency across their financial journeys. We believe that 
the future of banking will belong to institutions that can 
combine scale with personalisation, digital convenience 
with human support, and innovation with responsibility.
A central pillar of this strategy is the creation of a 
comprehensive 360-degree view of the customer. 
We are investing in data analytics and technology 
capabilities that provide a deeper understanding of 
customer needs, preferences, behaviours, lifecycle events, 
and financial aspirations. This approach enables us to move 
beyond product-led engagement towards relationship-
led banking. A holistic view of the customer allows our 
teams to offer more relevant solutions, anticipate service 
needs, identify opportunities for responsible cross-
sell, and provide timely assistance. It also helps reduce 
fragmentation in customer engagement, ensuring that 
customers experience AU SFB as one unified Bank rather 
than a collection of products or channels.
Our customer-centric strategy is also focused on 
delivering a differentiated omnichannel experience. 
Customers today expect convenience, speed, and 
consistency, but they also value trust, advice, and 
assurance, particularly in important financial decisions. 
Our approach is therefore digital-first, but not digital-only. 
We integrate physical, assisted and digital channels so 
that customers can engage with us through the channel of 
their choice. Branches, banking outlets, relationship teams, 
contact centres, video banking, mobile platforms, and 
assisted digital channels all have an important role to play 
in delivering a seamless customer experience. The aim is 
to ensure that when a customer starts a journey digitally, 
seeks support through an assisted channel or completes a 
transaction at a branch, the experience remains consistent, 
convenien

t and reliable.
Innovation in products and solutions will remain an 
important driver of customer engagement. 
We will continue to design segment-focused offerings that 
address specific financial needs and deepen customer 
relationships. This includes solutions that support savings, 
deposits, payments, credit, business banking, insurance, 
wealth, and other financial requirements across the 
customer lifecycle. By tailoring offerings to customer 
segments and use cases, we seek to enhance relevance 
and improve outcomes. Our focus is not merely on 
acquiring customers, but on building enduring relationships 
by becoming a trusted financial partner across life stages, 
business cycles, and evolving aspirations.
End-to-end journey automation is another  
key priority. 
We are focused on simplifying onboarding, servicing, and 
closure processes to reduce customer effort and improve 
turnaround times. Automation across customer journeys 
will help eliminate avoidable friction, improve process 
consistency, and strengthen service delivery across 
channels. It will also enable faster resolution of service 
requests, better tracking of customer interactions, and 
improved accountability within the organisation. As we 
grow, such automation will be critical to maintaining service 
quality at scale while ensuring that our frontline teams can 
spend more time on meaningful customer engagement.
Technology, data and artificial intelligence will play  
a central role in the next phase of customer experience 
transformation. 
We are building an AI-enabled service model that can 
improve responsiveness, accuracy and consistency 
across customer touchpoints. Capabilities such as voice 
bots, virtual assistants, AI-driven complaint management, 
knowledge engines, and agent-assist tools can help us 
deliver faster and more informed support to customers. 
These tools can also help our employees serve customers 
better by providing relevant information, guiding resolution, 
and reduc

ing dependency on manual processes. Our 
objective is to use technology to make banking simpler and 
more responsive, while ensuring that customers continue to 
experience care, transparency and accountability.
At the same time, we recognise that responsible use 
of technology is essential to preserving trust. As digital 
adoption expands and AI-led capabilities become more 
embedded in banking operations, customer protection, 
privacy, fairness, and transparency will remain central to 
our approach. Customer data must be used responsibly, 
with appropriate governance, security, and consent

Universal Banking and  
ease of business
We expect our potential transition to a universal Bank to 
be a structural step-change, rather than a mere change in 
nomenclature. It expands our addressable opportunity and 
unlocks several levers that can directly support our loan 
portfolio growth:
Technology and  
AI-led enablement
Technology and AI are increasingly becoming the 
operating layer through which AU SFB intends to 
scale growth, strengthen distribution and manage the 
complexity associated with its potential transition to a 
Universal Bank. During FY 2025-26, the Bank accelerated 
its investments in Agentic AI with a clear focus on 
enhancing productivity, improving customer experience 
and creating sustainable operating leverage.

»
Lower Priority Sector Lending (PSL) 
commitment:
As per regulatory norms, Small Finance Banks 
are currently required to allocate 60% of their 
Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to Priority 
Sector Lending (PSL) with focus on farmer 
financing, agriculture ecosystem, housing, 
education and MSME etc. This PSL requirement 
reduces meaningfully to 40% of ANBC upon 
our transition to a universal bank. This will 
reduce our operating intensity around PSL 
classification, documentation, and monitoring, 
allowing our underwriting and business teams 
to deploy bandwidth more productively towards 
growing the business. While our underlying 
customer segment and business segments are 
not expected to change much, focus will shift 
from more compliance driven lending to a more 
opportunity and credit driven decision making.
	
»
Removal of ticket-size restrictions:
In compliance with Reserve Bank of India (RBI) 
guidelines applicable to Small Finance Banks, we 
deploy a minimum of 50% of our loan portfolio 
in ticket sizes of up to ₹25 Lakh. On transition to 
a universal bank, while we will continue to cater 
t

o the small ticket size loans, the removal of this 
regulatory constraint will enable us to participate 
more fully in larger-ticket opportunities across 
Mortgages, Commercial Banking, and Corporate 
Relationships, areas where our current 
participation has been shaped by regulatory 
ceilings rather than a lack of capability.
	
»
Enhanced brand and counterparty acceptance: 
Once the transition to a universal Bank is 
complete, it is expected to improve our 
counterparty comfort, institutional credibility, 
and eligibility for government, public-sector, and 
large-corporate relationships. Over time, this 
can support both sides of our balance sheet-
improving our ability to source quality assets as 
well as deepening our liability relationships.
Importantly, this transition arrives after our core 
foundations have already been built. Our governance 
architecture, leadership depth, a unified core banking 
platform (post the erstwhile Fincare integration), and 
a distribution network that has nearly doubled over 
two years, are all firmly in place. The universal banking 
milestone therefore becomes an accelerator of our already-
strengthened franchise, rather than the starting point for 
capability-building.
Collectively, these investments are helping build a more 
intelligent and scalable operating model that improves 
productivity, enhances customer experience and supports 
higher business volumes and broader product offerings, 
while maintaining cost discipline and risk controls.

At the current stage of the Bank’s lifecycle, improving 
efficiency, enhancing productivity and strengthening 
operating leverage are strategic priorities. As the Bank 
scales across products, channels, geographies and 
customer segments, technology is a critical lever to simplify 
operations, reduce manual effort, improve turnaround 
times and deliver consistent outcomes at scale. The Bank’s 
technology strategy is therefore focused on two connected 
objectives: driving near-term productivity and efficiency, 
while building the foundation of a future-ready, tech-first 
organisation.
Artificial Intelligence will be an important enabler of this 
transformation. AI-led automation, intelligent workflows, 
real-time decisioning and data-dr

iven insights can 
help improve customer experience, strengthen risk 
management, enhance employee productivity and reduce 
cost-to-serve. The objective is not only to digitise existing 
processes, but to redesign them for speed, accuracy, 
scalability and control. 
To execute this agenda with focus and accountability, the 
Bank has built a strong technology foundation and is now 
scaling its strategy across three pillars: Run, Build and 
Transform with independent leadership, defined priorities 
and measurable KPIs for each team. This framework allows 
us to balance near-term reliability and execution discipline 
with long-term innovation and future readiness.
Run: Strengthen the 
Foundation
The Run pillar is focused on keeping the Bank’s core 
technology environment reliable, secure and efficient. 
As transaction volumes grow, the Bank will continue to 
strengthen resilience, scalability and availability across 
its infrastructure. Priorities include modernising core 
banking and payment systems, expanding cloud and hybrid 
infrastructure, strengthening API gateway and integration 
platforms, enhancing disaster recovery, upgrading identity 
and access management and deepening cyber resilience.
The Bank will also use AI-led IT operations, automated 
monitoring, observability frameworks, predictive incident 
management and centralised command centres to improve 
reliability and reduce disruption. The focus under Run 
is to maintain a stable, secure and scalable technology 
backbone, while improving efficiency across infrastructure, 
applications and support processes.
Build: Deliver a Digital-First and 
Data-Driven Bank
The Build pillar is focused on creating differentiated digital 
experiences for customers, employees and partners. 
The Bank will continue to enhance AU 0101 and AU 0101 
Business, while strengthening digital onboarding, employee 
workflows, commercial banking automation, digital CMS 
solutions and partner and fintech ecosystem APIs. The 
emphasis is

on seamless, intuitive and consistent journeys 
across retail, commercial and corporate banking.

Investments in real-time data pipelines, Customer 360

and workflow automation will support deeper customer

stronger risk controls and higher operating efficiency. Build 
will help reduce customer effort, improve turnaround times 
and create scalable platforms for future growth.
Transform: Build an AI-Powered, 
Future-Ready Bank
The Transform pillar represents the Bank’s ambition to 
become an AI-powered and intelligence-led institution. 
The Bank will progressively embed AI across onboarding, 
lending, underwriting, servicing, collections, fraud 
monitoring, compliance, engineering and internal 
operations. A dedicated AI Centre of Excellence will drive 
identification, prioritisation and scaling of high-impact use 
cases across the enterprise.
The Bank is also developing Agentic AI capabilities  
across voice, onboarding, lending, customer service, 
compliance and employee productivity, supported by 
robust data governance, model risk controls, cybersecurity 
safeguards, explainability, bias mitigation and responsible 
AI principles. Over time, the objective is to move towards 
an AI-native operating model where data, intelligence 
and automation are embedded across key business and 
operational processes.
At the same time, the Bank recognises that innovation must 
be accompanied by responsibility. As technology, data 
and AI become more deeply embedded in banking, the 
Bank will continue to prioritise cybersecurity, data privacy, 
model governance, explainability, bias mitigation and 
ethical adoption. Strong oversight, resilient architecture and 
responsible AI governance will be essential to maintaining 
customer trust and regulatory c

onfidence.
Together, these initiatives position the Bank to scale 
with greater efficiency, resilience and intelligence. By

will remain a decisive enabler of productivity, customer 
experience and long-term franchise strength as  
AU SFB advances towards a future-ready operating  
model sustainably.
A critical enabler of this strategy will be disciplined 
technology governance and sharper alignment between 
business priorities and technology execution. The 
Bank will focus on portfolio prioritisation, stronger 
program management, architecture standardisation, 
vendor accountability and benefits tracking to ensure 
that technology investments translate into measurable 
outcomes. This will include clearer ownership of initiatives, 
faster decision cycles, improved delivery discipline and 
stronger linkage between spend, risk, productivity and 
customer impact. By combining innovation with execution

a support function, but a strategic multiplier for growth, 
efficiency, control and enterprise-wide value creation.

Strong Governance and

Governance as a strategic 
foundation
Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) remains a critical 
cornerstone of the Bank given its role as a custodian of 
public deposits, supported by a well-established and 
institutionalised framework that upholds high standards 
of governance, transparency, and accountability. Strong 
governance and disciplined risk management provide the 
stability and confidence required to scale sustainably. 
As we progress towards becoming a universal banking 
franchise, our governance and risk management framework 
has been deliberately strengthened to keep pace with the 
increasing scale, complexity and responsibility of  
the institution.
The Reserve Bank of India’s in-principle approval for our 
transition to a Universal Bank in August 2025 is more than 
a regulatory milestone; it reflects the trust and confidence 
the Bank has built through years of consistent, transparent 
and accountable conduct.
Independence of Board and  
control functions
The governance framework is further strengthened by a 
balanced and diversified Board with a strong independent 
presence, enabling effective oversight, objective decision-
making, and prudent risk stewardship. Importantly, 
governance, risk, compliance, and audit functions operate 
as independent oversight mechanisms and are not driven 
by business targets, thereby minimising potential conflicts 
of interest and ensuring unbiased risk assessment and 
regulatory compliance.
Independence extends beyond the

Board to the control 
functions that sit beneath it. Risk, Compliance and 
Internal Audit operate independent of business lines 
each with clearly defined mandates, direct access to 
Board committees, and the authority to escalate without 
interference. The Head of Internal Audit reports directly to 
the Audit Committee, ensuring that assurance is objective 
and autonomous. Similarly, Chief Risk Officer (CRO) reports 
to the Risk Management Committee of the Board.
The Bank follows a well-defined Three Lines of Defence 
framework comprising business and control functions as 
the first line, independent Risk and Compliance functions 
as the second line, and Internal Audit as the third line, 
ensuring robust internal controls and multiple layers of 
oversight. Dedicated functions across Risk, Compliance, 
Internal Audit, Secretarial, and Vigilance continuously 
strengthen governance standards through comprehensive 
risk management, policy oversight, and control monitoring. 
The Bank will continue to enhance its enterprise-wide 
risk assessment framework, including credit, operational, 
market, liquidity, conduct, and emerging risks, supported by 
technology-enabled monitoring and advanced analytics.
	
»
Credit governance
Sound credit governance remains central to our 
credit risk management philosophy. The Credit Risk 
Committee, supported by clearly defined risk appetite 
frameworks and underwriting standards, oversees 
credit risk across our lending portfolio. Enhancing our 
credit decisioning capabilities through the adoption 
of AI-first platforms, enabling more consistent, data-
driven credit assessments and early risk detection 
remain key focus areas for the Bank.
Our ICAAP and periodic stress-testing exercises ensure 
that capital buffers remain adequate under adverse 
scenarios, and that credit risk concentrations are 
monitored proactively. The outcome of these processes 
are reported regularly to the Risk Management 
Committee and the Board.
	
»
Fraud preve

ntion and vigilance
We maintain a structured and multi-layered approach to 
fraud prevention and vigilance. The Special Committee 
of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of Cases 
provides Board-level oversight of fraud risk, reviewing 
root-cause analyses, monitoring recovery positions, 
and ensuring that systemic weaknesses are addressed 
through strengthened controls.
The Whistle Blower and Vigil Mechanism provide 
a formal channel for employees, customers, and 
stakeholders to report concerns with direct access to 
the Audit Committee Chairperson for escalation.  
No legitimate concern is left without a pathway  
to resolution.
	
»
Expanding risk management to emerging areas
Expanding our Enterprise Risk Management framework 
to address emerging risk categories alongside 
traditional financial risks remains a key priority. A 
partnership with the International Finance Corporation 
(IFC) to integrate climate risk into core banking strategy 
is a significant project which will help embedding 
physical and transition risk considerations into lending 
decisions and portfolio management.

Enhancing Portfolio Resilience Through 
Rethinking Credit Governance Architecture
India’s economic momentum is ushering in a new phase 
of sustained credit expansion, but one that is unfolding 
in a far more complex and rapidly evolving environment 
than seen before. Rising borrower leverage, the 
growing influence of digital lending, tighter regulatory 
expectations, frequent macroeconomic and geopolitical 
disruptions are collectively reshaping the risk landscape.
At AU Small Finance Bank (AU SFB), we recognise that 
the focus cannot simply be on growing the balance sheet, 
but on scaling in a manner that preserves asset quality 
and delivers predictable, risk-adjusted returns. This belief 
forms the foundation of our credit governance approach, 
where precision underwriting, disciplined risk alignment, 
and forward-looking monitoring are embedded at every 
stage of the credit lifecycle. 
Recognising this shift, we aligned the entire credit 
governance function under one umbrella and created the 
post of Chief Credit Officer (CCO) of the Bank. Under the 
CCO depa

rtment, we have consolidated underwriting, 
portfolio monitoring, asset quality, security enforcement, 
legal and collection architectures as well as credit policy. 
Our effort has been to build a credit model that is both 
sustainable and scalable. Sustainability is ensuring that 
portfolio behaviour remains stable across cycles, credit 
costs are predictable, and underwriting practices are fully 
aligned with regulatory and audit expectations. A key shift 
we have made is moving from a purely deal-level lens to a 
portfolio-centric view of risk, allowing us to assess not just 
individual exposures but also concentrations, correlations, 
and systemic vulnerabilities. At the same time, by being 
consistent across geographies and segments and 
adaptable to new products, scalability is being driven 
through data-led and digitally enabled decision-making.
We are consciously moving away from a one-size-fits-all 
approach to underwriting and adopting a more granular, 
segment-specific risk approach, recognising that each

borrower segment, across secured retail, micro, small 
and medium enterprises (MSME), commercial banking

, 
microfinance, and unsecured lending, has distinct risk 
drivers. Traditional inputs such as bureau behaviour, 
banking analysis, and financial statements are being 
complemented with alternate data like Goods and Services 
Tax (GST) trends, transaction analytics, and digital 
footprints. In cases where formal data is limited, alternate 
methods, including geographic risk profiling, industry 
cluster behaviour, and vintage performance trends are 
helping us to strengthen decision-making and improve 
coverage across customer segments.
Data-Led Underwriting: Combining bureau insights 
with GST trends, transaction analytics and digital 
footprints for sharper credit decisions.
We are building in risk-based pricing and more flexible 
limit setting into our processes, so that both pricing and 
exposure reflect the real risk of the borrower. Instead of 
applying a standard rate across customers, the approach 
is to adjust pricing based on the borrower’s risk profile, 
ensuring that returns remain appropriate for the level 
of risk being taken. Similarly, lending limits, especially 
in commercial banking, are increasingly aligned to the 
strength and stability of the borrower’s cash flows, rather 
than relying only on collateral. 
Risk-Based Pricing: Aligning pricing and lending  
limits with each borrower’s risk profile to optimise 
risk-adjusted returns.
Technology underpins this entire approach, with a focus 
on building an end-to-end credit decision engine that 
integrates rules, scorecards, and analytics. This supports 
a segmented underwriting flow, where low-risk cases are 
processed through Straight Through Processing (STP), 
moderate-risk through assisted underwriting, and higher-
risk exposures through detailed evaluation. Expanding STP, 
particularly in retail portfolios, is improving turnaround times 
and cost efficiency while maintaining consistency. We are 
also strengthening pre-approved and pre-qualified funnels, 
which help improve conversion and reduce

acquisition and 
underwriting costs.
Technology-Led Credit Decision: Integrating rules, 
scorecards, analytics and segmented underwriting for 
faster, more consistent credit decisions.
Recognising that risk evolves continuously, we are 
strengthening our early warning and monitoring capabilities 
using data and analytics, tracking real-time indicators 
such as banking behaviour changes, GST movements, 
credit bureau triggers, and EMI repayment patterns. These 
are linked to structured action frameworks that enable 
timely interventions, including customer engagement, limit 
recalibration, and targeted collections. In parallel, we are 
enhancing our focus on portfolio-level governance. Through 
internal monitoring frameworks, we track key indicators 
such as vintage performance, delinquency flow rates across 
buckets, segment-wise stress build-up, and geographic 
concentrations. This provides a forward-looking view of 
portfolio health and enables dynamic decision-making, 
including tightening credit filters or recalibrating exposures 
in segments where early signs of stress emerge.
Real-Time Risk Monitoring: Tracking behavioural, 
GST, bureau and repayment indicators to enable 
proactive portfolio management.
Moreover, we believe that credit culture is equally critical. 
We place strong emphasis on embedding risk ownership 
within business teams, supported by maker-checker 
discipline and clear communication of risk appetite. 
Decision-making is encouraged to be balanced and 
prudent, including the ability to decline opportunities that 
do not meet risk standards. This is reinforced through 
aligned performance metrics, where growth is evaluated 
alongside portfolio quality, early delinquency indicators, 
slippages, and credit costs, ensuring that accountability is 
built across the credit lifecycle. 
 
The key principle guiding our approach is the need 
to balance credit cost with the cost of doing credit. 
Excessively conservative underwriting can result in missed

opportunities and lower growth, while overly complex 
processes can increase operating costs and reduce 
efficiency. Our focus is on optimising the total cost of risk, 
which includes credit cost, origination cost, collection cost, 
and opportunity cost.

Scalable Growth Through Cross-Sell and 
Digital Acquisition
Cross-selling to our existing customer base (ETB)
and unlocking the full potential of our lead ecosystem 
represents one of the most capital-efficient growth levers 
at our disposal. With over 1.2 Crore customers across 
our deposit, asset and digital franchises, the opportunity 
to deepen relationships through additional products and 
services is both significant and largely untapped. We have 
adopted a resilient and focused approach on building a 
comprehensive, technology-enabled Cross-sell, Up-sell 
and Digital lead acquisition framework that brings together 
co-origination, referral and external lead streams of NTB 
customers into a single, analytics and AI-driven engine.
Building a scalable cross-sell and 
digital lead acquisition engine
Cross-sell and digital lead acquisition architecture 
framework is designed around three complementary 
opportunity pools: cross-sell, up-sell and digital lead 
acquisition, each supported by metadata, analytics and 
technology-led execution.
To support this framework of cross-sell and digital lead 
acquisition, we are building a centralised lead management 
and routing architecture. Leads from various sources are 
aggregated on a central data platform, qualified through 
analytics-based propensity models and scorecards and 
routed based on internal and external customer, lead 
quality, urgency and customer context.
	
»
Cross-sell opportunities are identified at the point of 
co-origination, enabling relevant product discovery 
when customer engagement is at its highest. These 
journeys are being embedded across our retail loan 
systems and liability platforms, allowing customers 
t

o receive a more holistic view of our offerings and 
enabling referrals across core journeys. 
Our lead management application for the sales  
team serves as the primary execution layer for self-
sourcing, cross-sell and lead assignment. Relationship 
managers can receive, manage and action leads 
through the platform, connect with customers directly 
from the interface and update customer interactions 
and dispositions. 
	
»
Up-sell focuses on deepening existing relationships 
within the same product vertical, such as encouraging 
savings account customers to open fixed deposits or 
offering enhanced loan eligibility to existing borrowers. 
Integration with Account Aggregator and other data 
sources provides real-time financial insights, helping us 
identify more relevant and timelier up-sell triggers for 
each customer.
	
»
Digital Lead Acquisition consolidates a wider 
funnel of externally sourced, referral-based and 
internally generated opportunities for NTB customers. 
Consolidation of all lead sources into a single platform 
allows us to monitor the engagement with each source 
in terms of lead flow and business conversion.

The Reserve Bank of India’s in-principle approval for AU 
SFB’s transition to a Universal Bank on August 7, 2025 
marked a defining milestone in our journey, reflecting nearly 
three decades of disciplined institution building. The Bank 
became the first Small Finance Bank in India to receive an 
in-principle Universal Banking license.  
 
The RBI recognised the Bank’s satisfactory track record 
and fulfilment of the eligibility criteria under the voluntary 
transition framework issued in April 2024. Pursuant to the 
Bank’s request, RBI replaced the requirement relating to 
the establishment of a Non-Operative Financial Holding 
Company (NOFHC). Under the revised condition, the 
requirement would arise only if the Bank or its promoter 
group seeks to es

tablish a group entity in the future, 
thereby streamlining the transition pathway. In March 
2026, the Bank submitted its final license application to the 
RBI, marking another significant step towards becoming a 
Universal Bank.
Progressing Towards Universal 
Banking
Expanding our opportunity
The potential transition to a Universal Bank significantly 
expands our strategic canvas. It broadens our addressable 
market, enhances operating flexibility and enables us to 
participate more comprehensively across our customers’ 
financial journeys. This creates opportunities to serve a 
wider spectrum of customer segments - including salaried 
professionals, affluent households, senior citizens, NRIs and 
larger commercial enterprises through an expanded suite 
of banking, payments, treasury, wealth management and 
transaction banking solutions.
The transition will remove several regulatory 
requirements associated with the Small Finance 
Bank framework, providing greater flexibility in 
portfolio construction, liability mobilisation and 
capital allocation, while enabling deeper and  
longer-lasting customer relationships. 
Strengthening  
long-term foundations
Beyond expanding business opportunities, universal 
banking license will enhance the structural 
strengths of the franchise. A broader deposit-
gathering capability, increased participation in 
government and institutional banking opportunities, 
wider market acceptance and greater refinancing 
flexibility collectively improve the resilience, 
diversification and scalability of the Bank.
The transition will also create additional avenues to 
drive operating leverage through greater flexibility 
across securitisation, co-lending and other  
strategic initiatives.
Importantly, we enter this phase from a position 
of strength. Over the years, we have consistently 
invested in technology, governance, risk 
management and operational capabilities aligned 
with Universal Banking standards. This transition will 
enable u

s to unlock the full potential of capabilities 
that have already been built and tested at scale.

The challenge
A merchant in a busy Rajasthan market was hesitant 
to adopt digital payments because he could not 
independently verify SMS confirmations. It was 
not distrust of technology that held him back. He 
simply could not read the SMS alerts that confirmed 
a payment had come through. Every digital 
transaction ended in a moment

of uncertainty he 
had no way to resolve, and so he stayed with cash.
The solution
We installed an AU QR Sound Box at his shop. The 
audio confirmation removed the need to interpret 
SMS alerts and reduced uncertainty at the point of 
payment.
The impact
The instant audio confirmation improved the 
merchant's confidence in digital transactions and 
encouraged regular usage. Today, the merchant 
is active within the formal digital payments 
ecosystem, with a transaction record that has 
improved his access to credit. It allowed him to 
expand his stock, and helped him grow his shop 
in ways he could not have imagined before. This 
illustrates how accessible technology can convert 
trust into measurable business outcomes.

Key Risks and Mitigation
We have established a strong risk culture and risk governance framework to enable risk assessment, identification, 
measurement, mitigation and reporting of risks within the Bank.
Key risks and their mitigation framework are as follows:
Credit risk management
Credit risk refers to the potential 
loss arising from a borrower’s or 
counterparty’s failure to meet their 
contractual obligations, including 
repayments, settlements, or other 
financial commitments.
Mitigation
The Credit Risk unit is responsible for assessing and monitoring credit risk via 
setting up thresholds, risk limits and closely tracking asset quality. It conducts 
periodic portfolio reviews, aligned with our evolving risk appetite and business 
plans. Oversight extends to credit strategy, underwriting and risk frameworks 
like early warning systems, portfolio triggers, risk classifications and high-value 
exposure monitoring. By adopting a forward-looking approach and leveraging 
data analytics, the Credit Risk function ensures resilience in a dynamic 
economic and regulatory environment, supporting our long-term sustainability.
We follow a robust credit risk architecture with defined policies and systems 
for both retail and commercial lending. While commercial loans are managed 
on a standalone basis as well as on portfolio basis, retail lending, due to its 
granularity, is largely managed on a portfolio basis. Emphasis is placed on 
diversification, prudent credit approvals, post-disbursement monitoring and 
corrective actions.
The Credit Risk Management Committee (CRMC) monitors large exposures, 
asset quality, and portfolio concentration. The CRMC reviews portfolio trends, 
sector-level exposures, and emerging stress indicators, ensuring timely and 
calibrated risk mitigation. Its findings are submitted to the Board-level Risk 
Management Committee every quarter.
Operational risk management
Operational r

isk, as defined by 
the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), 
refers to the risk of loss arising 
from inadequate or failed internal 
processes, people, systems, or 
external events. It includes legal 
risk but excludes strategic and 
reputational risks.
Mitigation
We manage operational risk through a Board-approved Operational Risk 
Management Policy supported by a robust framework covering governance, 
processes, and controls across all business verticals. The framework follows 
the three lines of defence model:
1.	 First Line: Business units, support functions, and operations
2.	 Second Line: Independent Operational Risk Management Department 
(ORMD)
3.	 Third Line: Internal Audit
The ORMD is responsible for implementing the operational risk framework 
across the Bank. Oversight is provided by the ORMC, which monitors 
effectiveness, reviews key risk issues, and recommends mitigation measures. 
The ORMC reports to the RMC, ensuring effective Board-level supervision and 
governance. 
Fraud risk management
Fraud risks are managed through a dedicated Fraud Control Unit (FCU) 
operating under a Board-approved Fraud Risk Management Policy. The FCU is 
responsible for identification, investigation, and containment of fraud incidents 
across the Bank. Oversight of significant fraud cases is provided by the Special 
Committee of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of Cases of Fraud 
(SCBMF), which reviews root cause analyses and monitors the implementation 
of corrective and preventive actions.
We continuously strengthen our systems and monitoring capabilities through 
real-time transaction surveillance, enhanced internal controls, and increased

staff vigilance. Regular training and awareness programmes are conducted 
to sensitise employees to emerging fraud risks and reinforce a culture of 
accountability and prevention. 
Outsourcing risk management

aligned with RBI gui

delines. While the Board retains ultimate responsibility for 
outsourcing arrangements, operational oversight is delegated to the Committee 
for Outsourcing of IT and Financial Services, which reports to the RMC. The

Business continuity management

which is periodically reviewed to remain aligned with regulatory requirements 
and evolving risk scenarios. The framework includes dedicated Disaster

simulations and drills are used to continuously strengthen resilience and ensure 
continuity of critical operations during disruptions.

The world economy, which was broadly resilient in 2025, is facing renewed headwinds, primarily due to geopolitical 
tensions, particularly the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. As a baseline scenario, the IMF’s April 2026 World Economic 
Outlook has projected global growth at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027, which is below the long-term historical average 
growth of 3.7%. However, in a more adverse scenario involving prolonged conflict, growth could fall to approximately 2.5%. 
In a se

vere scenario with significant disruption to global energy supplies or trade routes, growth could even drop to 2%, 
approaching recessionary conditions.
Global Economy on Edge
Inflation has re-emerged as a key concern, with global 
inflation projected to rise to about 4.4% in 2026 before 
moderating to around 3.7% in 2027. The uptick in inflation is 
largely attributed to higher energy prices and supply chain 
disruptions, especially those affecting critical trade routes. 
This has complicated the task of central banks, which 
now face an intense trade-off between maintaining tight 
monetary policy to control inflation and easing policy rates 
to support weakening growth.
As regards the growth outlook, risks are skewed to 
the downside. Key risks include further escalation of 
geopolitical tensions, persistently high oil prices, increasing 
trade fragmentation and protectionist measures, tightening 
global financial conditions, and high levels of public debt 
that limit fiscal space. There are some upside possibilities, 
such as stronger-than-expected gains from artificial 
intelligence or a faster easing of geopolitical tensions. 
Signing of MoU between the US and Iran for a ceasefire 
is considered to be a positive development, which is 
expected to normalise crude oil prices to the pre-war level 
if sanctions are removed against Iran on an enduring basis.
From a policy perspective, maintaining a credible monetary 
policy to anchor inflation expectations, even as growth 
slows, assumes importance. Globally, there is also a need 
to rebuild fiscal buffers, given elevated debt levels, and 
strengthen international cooperation to address shared 
challenges such as trade disruptions and energy security. 
Structural reforms aimed at boosting productivity, including 
through digitalisation and innovation, are also critical for 
medium-term growth.

domestic demand and robust services exports, making it 
the fastest-growing major economy.
Broadly, the global economy is navigating a fragile phase 
marked by slowing growth, persistent inflation pressures, 
and elevated uncertainty. Geopolitical developments have 
become the dominant influence on the economic outlook, 
and the balance of risks remains tilted to the downside, 
requiring cautious and coordinated policy responses.

India’s macroeconomic performance in FY 2025-26 
remained robust. According to the provisional estimates 
by the NSO, India’s real GDP growth was 7.7% in FY 
2025-26, supported by strong domestic demand, resilient 
activity in the services sector, and sustained public capital 
expenditure. The economy demonstrated resilience despite 
global headwinds such as elevated global uncertainties, 
geopolitical tensions, reciprocal tariffs by the US, and 
commodity price volatility.
Private consumption showed steady improvement during 
the year, aided by easing inflation, rising rural incomes, 
and stable urban demand. Government capital expenditure 
continued to play a critical role in sustaining growth 
momentum, particularly through infrastructure development 
in transport, logistics, and energy sectors. Investment 
activity remained mixed, with public investment strong 
while private corporate investment showed gradual but 
uneven recovery, reflecting cautious business sentiment 
amid global uncertainties.
Inflation dynamics improved in FY 2025-26, with headline 
CPI inflation moderating to 2.1% compared to 4.6% in t

he 
previous year, mainly due to deflation in food prices in 
Q2 and Q3 of FY 2025-26. Core inflation showed signs of 
stickiness due to metal prices. The underlying inflation was 
weak as core inflation without gold and silver prices was 
extremely benign at 2.1%. The RBI maintained a neutral 
monetary policy stance since June 2025.
On the external front, India’s position remained manageable. 
While merchandise trade balance faced headwinds from 
the US tariff, higher crude oil prices, weak global demand 
and supply disruptions, services exports, especially in 
IT and business services, and remittances continued to 
provide strong support to the external current account. The 
Current Account Deficit (CAD) remained comfortable at 
0.6% of GDP in FY 2025-26 aided by resilient remittances 
and IT-enabled services. As capital flows were insufficient 
to finance the CAD, the exchange rate was under pressure, 
particularly towards the end of the year. Foreign exchange 
reserves remained comfortable, providing an adequate 
buffer against external shocks.
Fiscal policy continued to focus on consolidation while 
supporting growth. The central government adhered to its 
medium-term fiscal consolidation path, reducing the fiscal 
deficit gradually while maintaining high-quality expenditure, 
particularly on infrastructure. Tax revenues performed 
well, supported by strong economic activity and improved 
compliance, while subsidy burdens remained contained 
despite volatility in global commodity prices.

Outlook for FY 2026-27
The outlook for FY 2026-27 is clouded by external 
headwinds. Although India’s GDP growth is projected 
lower in the range of 6.5-6.7%, India will continue to be 
the fastest growing major economy in the world. Domestic 
demand is expected to remain the primary growth driv

er, 
supported by continued public investment, gradual 
strengthening in private investment, and sustained 
consumption demand.
However, risks to the outlook persist. Key external risks 
include prolonged geopolitical tensions, elevated global 
energy prices, and tighter global financial conditions, 
which could impact capital flows and the external balance. 
Domestically, inflation risks, particularly from food and 
fuel, remain a concern and could influence public policy 
responses. The RBI, in its June monetary policy, has 
projected retail Inflation higher at 5.1% in FY 2026-27. The 
current account deficit (CAD) is expected to widen in  
FY 2026-27.	
Both the government and RBI have taken several steps 
to minimise the adverse effects of the West Asia conflict. 
Short-term measures by the government include, inter 
alia, increase in import duties on precious metals, limited 
pass-through of petroleum prices to consumers, temporary 
ban on sugar exports, credit guarantee scheme for MSME 
lending, waiving withholding tax and capital gain tax on 
investment by FIIs/BIS in G-secs, besides encouraging 
domestic production of pulses and oilseeds etc., through 
a steep hike in MSP of farm products that are imported. 
Medium-term initiatives by the government relate to coal 
gasification, oil and gas exploration involving multi-national 
corporations, push for electric and flex-fuel vehicles, 
creation of strategic oil reserves involving investment 
from the UAE, interest subvention scheme for production 
of e-buses and e-trucks, promotion of bio-refineries, and 
expediting FTAs with multiple countries.
The RBI has also taken several regulatory measures to 
relieve pressure on the rupee. Notable among them are 
relaxation of external commercial borrowings, providing 
concessional forex swap for External Commercial 
Borrowings (ECB) by PSUs and Overseas Foreign Currency 
Borrowings by authorised dealers (ADs) till December 31, 
2026, absorbing hedging cost of NRI deposi

ts mobilised 
under FCNR route by ADs for three to five years up to 
September 30, 2026, besides widening the scope of 
portfolio investments in equity and debt by overseas 
investors.   
Policy priorities for the period ahead include maintaining 
macroeconomic stability while fostering inclusive growth. 
Continued fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted capital 
expenditure, will be essential. On the monetary side, the 
focus remains on achieving durable price stability while 
ensuring adequate liquidity to support growth. Structural 
reforms aimed at enhancing productivity, promoting 
manufacturing competitiveness, boosting exports, and 
leveraging digitalisation will be key to sustaining high 
growth over the medium term.
India enters 2026-27 from a position of relative strength, 
with solid growth fundamentals, stable macroeconomic 
conditions, and a resilient financial system. While external 
uncertainties pose challenges, the domestic growth engine 
remains strong, underpinning India’s status as a leading 
driver of global economic growth.
Financial sector conditions remained stable in FY 2025-26, with banks maintaining healthy balance sheets.  
Non-performing assets of scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) declined further, and credit growth remained strong, 
particularly in retail and services segments. Capital adequacy ratios improved, although there was some moderation in 
profitability as compared to last year. Liquidity coverage ratio at 124.2% was above the regulatory requirement, although 
slightly lower than 132.5% a year ago. Net interest margin was under pressure (3.3% in March 2026 as compared to 3.5% 
in March 2025). Both return on assets and return on equity of SCBs slightly moderated.  
Financial markets, however, experienced intermittent volatility due to global factors, including shifts in risk sentiment  
and capital flows. The rupee was under pressure, primarily due to portfolio outflows and surge in crude oil prices. India’s 
10-year benchmark

yield remained elevated, particularly in Q4 2025-26 (around 7%). However, gap between India’s 
benchmark yield and the US 10-year yield narrowed in FY 2025-26. Since the US-Iran MoU, the financial market conditions 
have been normalising globally with its impact felt in India too.

heading downwards with RBI cutting benchmark repo rate 
by 125 bps between February 2025 and March 2026. This 
resulted in a decline in yields on ~28% of the variable-
rate loan book as most of this book was linked to the repo 
rate. Additionally, there was also a shift in asset mix with a 
degrowth in the high-yield unsecured book. Together, this 
led to moderation in loan yields of ~50 bps to 13.9% in  
FY 2025-26 as compared to 14.4% in FY 2024-25.
Lower yields on loans were partially offset by a reduction in 
term deposit rates. Timely deposit rate reductions helped 
lower the average cost of funds by 32 basis points to  
6.

75% in FY 2025-26, as compared with 7.07% in the 
previous year.  
Consequently, Net Interest Margin (NIM) for FY 2025-
26 stood at 5.65% as against 5.94% in FY 2024-25. 
While margins moderated due to repricing of assets, we 
continued to benefit from strong balance sheet growth and 
as a result, NII increased by 14% Y-o-Y to ₹9,113 Crore in 
FY 2025-26, as compared with ₹8,012 Crore in FY 2024-25.
Other Income

Crore in FY 2025-26, supported by broad-based growth 
across fee and treasury streams. General Banking and 
cross-sell related fees grew strongly by 25% to ₹871 Crore. 
Transaction Banking and Forex income also witnessed

low base. Reflecting the declining interest rate environment, 
income from Treasury operations recorded robust growth 
of 65% to ₹389 Crore, contributing meaningfully to overall 
non-interest income. While Credit Card income remained 
subdued during FY 2025-26, a revival in credit card growth 
is expected to elevate the credit card fees going forward.
As a result, other income improved to 33% of Net Interest 
Income, reflecting continued diversification of our revenue 
mix and strengthening of fee-based income streams.

Wheels
The Wheels business has been our flagship franchise 
since inception in 1996 and continues to be the largest 
contributor within the retail secured portfolio, with the 
portfolio growing 27% Y-o-Y to ₹46,363 Crore as of 
March 31, 2026. The business is anchored in financing 
income-generating assets across rural and semi-urban 
markets, catering to customers engaged in transportation, 
agriculture and small business activities.
The portfolio spans a diversified set of segments including 
personal vehicles, commercial vehicles (across SCVs, LCVs, 
M&HCVs, three-wheelers and construction equipment)  
and tractors, enabling participation across multiple use-
cases while maintaining a balanced product mix. The 
customer base primarily comprises small and marginal 
farmers, self-employed individuals, MSMEs and transport 
operators, many of whom operate with limited formal 
income documentation.
A key strength of the franchise lies in its underwriting 
framework, which combines detailed field-level assessment 
with household cash flow analysis and business activity 
evaluation, supplemented by bureau data where available. 
This enables us to serve both formal and informal customer 
segments while maintaining strong credit discipline.  
Loans are structured against productive assets, with 
repayment capacity closely linked to asset utilisation  
and income generation.
The business is supported by a granular distribution 
network built on deep local presence and relationship-led 
sourcing, enabling high-quality origination, strong customer 
engagement and effective collections. 
Portfolio construction remains diversified across 
geographies, customer segments and asset classes, with a 
calibrated mix of new vehicles, used vehicles and refinance  
exposures to

manage cyclicality and ensure resilience 
across economic cycles.
Distribution expansion remained the primary initiative 
during FY 2025-26, with touchpoints nearly doubling over 
the last two years to around 1,000 locations. At the same 
time, the origination workflow has been fully migrated to 
Salesforce-based Loan Origination Systems and a FICO-
driven Business Rule Engine, enabling end-to-end straight-
through processing and improved underwriting consistency. 
AI-enabled enhancements are currently being developed  
to further reduce turnaround times and strengthen 
decisioning frameworks.
Progressing with industry trends, we have also introduced 
electric vehicle financing during the year, expanding its 
presence in emerging segments. Overall, the Wheels 
business continues to scale with a focus on disciplined 
underwriting, granular portfolio build-up and stable asset 
quality, supported by strong operating controls and 
continuous monitoring.
Going forward, this business will continue to deepen rural 
distribution while extending reach into South and East 
India markets, leveraging the geographic footprint gained 
through the erstwhile Fincare integration. Volume growth 
remains the primary objective, with active management 
of the product and customer mix to sustain yields and 
portfolio quality. The AI origination journey underway is 
anticipated to improve sourcing efficiency and reduce  
per-loan operating costs.

disciplined execution.

Inclusive Banking
We are committed to fostering financial inclusion by 
empowering the unbanked and underbanked individuals 
including small and marginal farmers, dairy farmers, small 
and micro animal husbandry enterprises, micro businesses, 
informal sector players, unrecognised entities especially 
in rural India. The Inclusive Finance portfolio comprises of 
Microfinance, Farmer Producer Organisations, and Small 
and Marginal Farmer loans, aimed at bridging the gap 
between underserved communities and formal banking 
segments through a comprehensive suite of tailored 
financial solutions and services such as microfinance loans, 
savings acc

ounts, deposit accounts, insurance products, 
direct benefit transfer linkages, AePS service and ATMs.
By combining innovative technology with efficient 
operations, we deliver accessible and affordable financial 
services, enabling individuals and businesses to build 
stability, resilience, and long-term prosperity. With over 
15 years of expertise in microloans, we have gained 
deep insights into the financial needs and aspirations of 
microloan borrowers and have built a strong presence in 
rural markets. As of March 31, 2026, we have established a 
widespread reach across 18 states, 347 districts, 58,000+ 
villages, serving 20 Lakh+ base-of-pyramid households and 
managing 49 Lakh+ rural savings accounts.
We follow a joint-liability group-based lending model, 
ensuring accessible credit solutions for rural communities. 
It facilitates loan disbursals and monthly collections while 
also conducting doorstep financial literacy camps. These 
initiatives reinforce our commitment to empowering rural 
borrowers through structured micro-lending and financial 
education. In rural areas, our key competitive advantage 
lies in providing comprehensive loan products throughout 
the lifecycle of rural customers, facilitated by our best-in-
class digital tools.
FY 2025-26 was a year of recovery for the microfinance 
industry as it emerged from the overleverage crisis of FY 
2024-25. It was a tale of two halves with H1-FY 2025-26 
seeing a 17% de-growth in the business with some recovery 
seen in H2-FY 2025-26. Overall, the MFI portfolio grew by  
a mere 3% during the year to close ₹6,879 Crore as of 
March 31, 2026.
The collection efficiency for non-overdue loans improved  
to 99.7% in Q4 FY 2025-26 and 92% of the overall book  
on March 31, 2026 was covered under the Credit  
Guarantee for Micro Units (CGFMU) scheme of the 
Government of India.
Our strategic emphasis on rural and microloan segments 
reinforces our commitment to financial inclusion while 
providing distinct co

mpetitive advantages, such as lower 
credit penetration, limited competition, strong customer 
loyalty, disciplined credit behaviour, and lower delinquency 
rates. With a proven track record in loan origination 
and servicing, supported by an extensive network of 
banking outlets and business correspondents, we are 
well-positioned to capitalise on growth opportunities and 
strengthen our presence in these underserved markets.
Our robust presence, customer-centric approach,  
best-in-class digital technology tools, evolved risk and 
credit framework, superior collections track record and 
focus on rural microloan segments contribute to our 
competitive advantage and position the Bank for continued 
growth in these areas. We have adopted and implemented 
the right strategic steps in a dynamic market environment 
by using our expertise and vintage team in rural markets.

B.	 Business overview
The FY 2025-26 reflected a year of sustained macroeconomic strength, with India’s growth supported by resilient domestic 
fundamentals despite an increasingly uncertain global environment. The most consequential shift of the year was on inflation 
where the headline consumer price inflation moderated sharply, easing the burden on household budgets and creating space 
for improved real purchasing power across income groups. The Reserve Bank of India (‘RBI’) responded by delivering a series

of policy rate cuts and injecting substantial durable liquidity into the system. 
On the fiscal side, the Union Budget introduced direct tax relief for the middle class while sustaining the government's 
public capital expenditure programme, together providing a dual boost to both consumption and investment. Rural demand 
emerged as a bright spot, supported by a favourable monsoon, stable agricultural incomes and rising real wages, while urban 
consumption also recovered on the back of tax rationalisation measures. The banking sector ended the year in its strongest 
condition in over a decade, with non-performing assets declining to multi-decade lows and profitability improving across the 
system. India's improving macro credibility was also recognised internationally, with the country receiving a sovereign credit 
rating upgrade during the year reflecting confidence in its fiscal discipline and structural reform momentum. 
While global uncertainties, including geopolitical developments and energy price volatility, persisted, India’s stable financial 
system and continued policy support enabled it to maintain a steady growth momentum.
Against this backdrop, the Bank delivered resilient and broad-based growth across its franchise, with deposits increasing by 
23% year-on-year to ₹1,52,661 Crore and gross loan portfolio growing by 21% year-on-year to ₹1,40,327 Crore. The liability 
franchise continued to strengthen, with stable deposits constituting 79% of total deposits and cost of funds declining by 
32 bps during FY 2025-26 to 6.75%, reflecting the Bank’s continued focus on granularity, stability and funding efficiency. 
Profitability improved meaningfully during the year, with profit after tax rising by 25% year-on-year to ₹2,641 Crore, return 
on assets improving to 1.6%, and return on equity to 14.2%. 
Asset quality strengthened over the course of the year as stress in unsecured portfolios normalised and secured businesses 
saw seasonal recovery. Gross NPA imp

roved to 2.03%, net NPA stood at 0.74%, and credit cost for FY 2025-26 moderated 
to 1.0% of average assets as compared with 1.3% in FY 2024-25. The Bank’s asset book remained well diversified and 
predominantly secured, with secured retail and commercial portfolios continuing to drive growth. 
A major strategic milestone during the year was the Bank’s progress towards transition into a Universal Bank. The Bank became 
the first Small Finance Bank to receive in-principle approval from the RBI for such transition, and subsequently, pursuant to 
the Bank’s request, the condition relating to the promoter holding structure was revised so that the Non Operative Financial 
Holding Company (‘NOHFC’) requirement would apply only if the Bank or its promoter group proposes to establish any group 
entity in the future. Following this, the Bank filed its application with the RBI in March 2026 for grant of the final licence for 
Universal Bank transition which is subject to regulatory approvals.
The year also saw notable progress in technology-led transformation. The Bank rolled out its first agentic AI platform with 
embedded guardrails and control frameworks, launched the gold loan origination journey on this AI-native platform, and 
continued to embed AI across customer engagement, underwriting, collections, internal productivity and workflow automation. 
The Bank also completed the migration of the core banking system of erstwhile Fincare Small Finance Bank into AU Small 
Finance Bank, resulting in a unified CBS, while revamping the AU0101 app and refreshing its website to improve customer 
experience and scalability. 
During FY 2025-26, the Bank continued to deepen and diversify its distribution footprint by adding new branches and 
touchpoints across geographies, with a focus on deepening presence in key markets including South India and expanded 
product distribution significantly across key businesses such as Wheels, Mortgages and Gold Loans. As at March 31, 2026, 
the B

ank served over 1.20 Crore customers through 2,790 touchpoints across 21 states and 4 union territories, supported 
by a workforce of 59,207 dedicated employees and a technology-led operating model built for scale, the Bank stands at the 
threshold of its most consequential chapter yet poised to grow not just in size, but in purpose and impact.
C.	 Dividend and dividend distribution policy
Pursuant to Regulation 43A of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (‘Listing Regulations’) 
and RBI guidelines, the Bank has formulated and adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy. The Policy is designed to achieve an 
optimal balance between rewarding shareholders through distribution of profits and retaining sufficient earnings to support 
the Bank’s sustainable growth and capital requirements.
In line with the aforementioned policy and considering the Bank’s financial performance during the FY 2025-26, the Board at 
its meeting held on April 27, 2026 recommended a dividend of 10% (₹1 per fully paid-up Equity Share of ₹10 each) for the year 
ended March 31, 2026. This recommendation will be placed before the shareholders for approval at the upcoming Annual 
General Meeting (‘AGM’) of the Bank.
Pursuant to RBI (Small Finance Banks-Prudential Norms for Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026, applicable from 
FY 2026-27, the Policy was reviewed and amended by the Board. The same can be viewed on the Bank's website at 
https://www.au.bank.in/investors/secretarial-policies.

The Bank remains deeply committed to environmental sustainability, consistently advancing initiatives aimed at reducing 
its carbon footprint. By leveraging digital technologies and implementing targeted emission-reduction strategies across its 
operations, the Bank continues to foster eco-conscious practices and contribute meaningfully to a greener future.
(a)	 Conservation of energy
Energy conservation at the Bank is approached through a combination of operational discipline, technology-led 
optimisation, and a progressive transition towards cleaner energy sources. Across offices and branches, initiatives are 
designed to minimise avoidable electricity consumption, enhance the efficiency of cooling and lighting systems, and 
strengthen monitoring mechanisms for informed decision-making.
In parallel, the Bank remained committed to sustainability through investments in renewable energy infrastructure and 
the promotion of sustainable finance solutions. These initiatives extend the Bank’s impact beyond internal operations, 
supporting the broader transition towards a low-carbon economy. Such efforts are aligned with the objectives of 
SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 13 (Climate Action), while also contributing to national priorities relating 
to renewable energy expansion and clean mobility.
1.	
Steps taken and impact on conservation of ene

rgy
The Bank’s approach is anchored in practical, site-level interventions that directly influence day-to-day energy consumption:
•	
Optimisation of cooling demand
Indoor green cover and plants have been promoted across premises to improve microclimate conditions and reduce 
heat load. This is complemented by maintaining air-conditioning temperatures at 25°C or higher, encouraging 
responsible energy use. These combined nature-based and behavioural interventions contribute to overall energy 
efficiency.
•	
Lighting efficiency improvements
Conventional lighting systems are being progressively replaced with energy-efficient LED fixtures, resulting in lower 
electricity consumption and improved lighting performance.
•	
Automation and control measures
Timers and automated controls have been deployed for signage and non-essential lighting to ensure that energy 
usage is linked to operational need, thereby reducing avoidable energy consumption.
•	
Power factor optimisation
Power factor correction systems have been implemented across electrical panels to improve electricity utilisation, 
reduce technical losses, and enhance overall energy efficiency and grid performance.

efficient infrastructure:

and optimisation of electricity consumption. This intervention has improved visibility into energy usage patterns 
and contributed to the optimisation of consumption.

Efficient cooling systems
Adoption of Variable Refrigerant Volume-based chiller systems has enhanced air-conditioning efficiency, delivering 
energy savings of up to 20% compared to conventional systems.

Reduction in diesel dependency

has reduced reliance on diesel 
generators, thereby lowering fossil fuel consumption and associated emissions while improving energy reliability.

Z.	 Risk Management
The Bank has invested significantly in elevating every dimension of its risk architecture from governance and Board oversight 
to technology-enabled risk surveillance, culture, and regulatory alignment. 
There is a well-institutionalised ‘Three Lines of Defence model’ Business units own risk management and internal controls, the 
Risk and Compliance function provides independent oversight and policy frameworks, and Internal Audit delivers objective 
assurance to the Board.
The Bank has instituted a comprehensive Enterprise Risk Management Framework (‘ERM’) that includes a strong governance 
structure, with the Board of Directors at its helm, Board Committees (including the Risk Management Committee of the Board), 
and executive committees of management for specialised risk-related aspects. 
Risk governance at the Bank is driven by the Board of Directors, which oversees the risk management framework and reviews 
the effectiveness of the material risk management systems. The Board is supported by the Risk Management Committee of 
the Board and other executive management-level committees constituted for specific risk areas.
The Chief Risk Officer (‘CRO’) functions independently and reports directly to the Risk Management Committee of the Board 
(‘RMC’), with no reporting lines to business verticals and without any dual responsibilities. This independent reporting structure 
ensures objective oversight and effective challenge of risk-management activities across the Bank. The Bank’s risk management 
function is supported by a dedicated team of professionals, who supervise and manage risk across the organisation.
The ERM Framework further comprises the Risk Appetite Statement (‘RAS’), covering various risk limits, risk policies and 
procedures, risk reports, Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (‘ICAAP’), and stress testing. This framework is 
designed to enhance the Bank’s ability to identify, monitor, mitigat

e, and report all types of risks in a timely and holistic manner. 
This ERM model encapsulates both financial and non-financial risk categories, including Credit Risk, Market and Liquidity 
Risk, Compliance Risk, Operational and Fraud Risk, People Risk, and Information Technology and Information Security Risk
Risk Appetite and Strategic Alignment
The Risk Appetite Statement serves as an important governance tool for aligning strategic decision-making with prudent 
risk-taking. The Risk Appetite Statement (‘RAS’), as approved and periodically reviewed by the Board, sets out the nature 
and extent of risk that the Bank is willing to assume in pursuit of its strategic and business objectives. It is integrated with 
business planning and capital management and is operationalised through defined limits, escalation thresholds and key risk 
indicators across relevant portfolios and functions.
Capital adequacy framework and stress testing
The Bank has adopted a Board-approved ICAAP and Stress Testing Policy as part of its capital management and risk 
governance framework. The RAS governs the Bank’s capital adequacy approach, and periodic stress-testing is undertaken 
to assess the resilience of capital adequacy, earnings and risk thresholds under base, adverse and severe stress scenarios. 
The outcomes of such assessments are reviewed through the Bank’s governance framework and are used to support prudent 
capital planning and risk mitigation measures.
In addition, while the regulatory capital charge requirements for market risk and operational risk are not applicable to Small 
Finance Banks, the Bank has, as a matter of prudent risk management, incorporated these risk categories within its ICAAP 
and stress-testing framework. The Bank continues to remain adequately capitalised under all relevant scenarios pertaining 
to its scale and nature of operations.
Risk categories, limits, thresholds and monitoring
The Bank’s comprehensive risk management framework ensures prudent i

dentification, monitoring, mitigation, and reporting 
of risks across the organisation. The framework covers key risk domains, including Credit Risk, Asset Liability Management 
(‘ALM’), Market Risk, Operational Risk, Cyber Security Risk, and Information Technology Risk. The RAS prescribes the 
Bank’s appetite/limits for various metrics for these risk categories. These limits are duly reviewed and presented to the Risk 
Management Committee of the Board on a quarterly basis.

The Bank has put in place detailed Board-approved risk management policies, frameworks, and internal risk limits for the key 
risks as detailed below. These internal thresholds are more stringent than the applicable regulatory requirements. Adherence 
to these limits, along with liquidity, deposit, and key regulatory ratios, is regularly monitored and reported to the RMC.
•	
Credit Risk: The Bank manages credit risk through portfolio-level and obligor-level controls, including internal limits 
relating to borrower, product and geographic concentrations, ticket-size mix, exposure limits to sensitive sectors, 
unsecured exposures (overall and product-wise), asset quality metrics and with limits on consumer credit exposures. 
The Bank has a well-developed, strong framework for Early Warning Signals (‘EWS’) for early identification of credit 
weakness in the portfolio across all ticket sizes through various risk checks like early delinquency, bouncing in repayments, 
external rating downgrade etc. through an automated EWS system for identification of weak/red-flagged accounts.
•	
Asset Liability Management and Market Risk: The Bank monitors the set internal limits and thresholds relating to 
liquidity and market risk, including liquidity coverage ratio, net stable funding ratio, earnings at risk, market value of 
equity, value at risk, PV01 for investment portfolios, modified duration, net overnight open position and stop-loss limits 
for the investment and foreig

n exchange books, as applicable.
•	
Operational Risk: Operational risk is managed through an established framework addressing the risk of loss arising from 
inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events. The Bank monitors operational 
loss events and fraud-related incidents arising from digital or physical channels through defined thresholds, control 
mechanisms and periodic review processes. The framework has been implemented covering third-party risk management, 
including financial and information technology outsourcing arrangements.
•	
Operational Resilience and Business Continuity: The Bank has a Board-approved Business Continuity Plan Policy aimed 
at preserving continuity of critical operations in the event of disruptions arising from system outages, infrastructure 
failures, process breakdowns or external events. Periodic business continuity testing is undertaken, and the results 
thereof are reviewed through the governance framework to strengthen operational resilience and preparedness.
•	
Technology Risk: During the year, the Bank continues to strengthen its technology risk management framework to 
address risks relating to technology infrastructure, critical systems and applications, business continuity and disaster 
recovery, information technology vendor management, change and project implementation, and associated people and 
process dependencies. Monitoring mechanisms include oversight of system availability, critical access controls and 
other key technology risk indicators.
•	
Information Security Risk: Information security risk management is led by the Chief Information Security Officer 
(‘CISO’) who reports directly to the Managing Director and CEO, thereby ensuring independence and robust oversight of 
information security risks. The CISO is supported by a dedicated team and an established cyber and information security 
framework. The Bank continues to strengthen its control environment, technology safeguar

ds, monitoring processes, 
and response capabilities to protect its information assets, systems, and digital infrastructure against unauthorised 
access, cyber threats, and service disruptions.
The Bank has consistently invested in advanced security tools and skilled manpower, commensurate with its scale of 
operations and evolving risk environment. The Bank has not faced or encountered any major cybersecurity incidents 
during the last financial year, reflecting the effectiveness and maturity of its information security controls and governance 
framework. 
•	
Environmental, Social and Governance (‘ESG’) Risks: As the Bank prepares itself for transition to a Universal Bank, 
responsible growth remains central to its strategy. The Bank continued to strengthen its framework for the identification, 
assessment, and management of ESG risks, including climate-related physical and transition risks, recognising their 
potential impact on asset quality, operational resilience, and long-term sustainability. ESG considerations are being 
progressively integrated into credit appraisal, risk assessment, and portfolio monitoring processes, guided by the SEBI 
BRSR framework, the GRI Standards, the RBI’s Master Direction on Climate Finance, 2025, and the Bank’s 4S Sustainability 
Framework, i.e., Sustainable Finance, Sustainable Operations, Sustainable Communities, and Sustainability Reporting.

AP.	 Status of Ind AS Implementation
As per the RBI circular no. RBI/2015‑16/315 DBR.BP.BC.No.76/21.07.001/2015‑16 dated February 11, 2016 on the implementation 
of Indian Accounting Standards (‘Ind AS’), banks are advised to follow Ind AS, as notified under the Companies (Indian 
Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, subject to guidelines or directions issued

by the RBI in this regard.
Banks in India currently prepare their financial statements in accordance with the guidelines issued by the RBI, the Accounting 
Standards notified under Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, and generally accepted accounting principles in India 
(‘Indian GAAP’). In January 2016, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs issued the roadmap for implementation of Ind AS, which are 
converged with International Financial Reporting Standards (‘IFRS’), for scheduled commercial banks, insurance companies and 
non‑banking financial companies. In March 2019, the RBI deferred the implementation of Ind AS for banks until further notice, 
as the recommended legislative amendments were under consideration by the Government of India. The Bank has undertaken 
a preliminary diagnostic assessment of differences between Indian GAAP and Ind AS and will progress implementation in line 
with applicable requirements and regulatory directions.

Bank’s governance structure
Consistent with the Reserve Bank of India’s (‘RBI’) expectations of Board-driven governance, enhanced fiduciary responsibility 
towards depositors, and strong oversight of risk, compliance and conduct, the Bank’s governance framework emphasises 
outcome-oriented supervision, robust assurance functions, and a culture of accountability led from the top.

serves as a trustee for all stakeholders, including shareholders, regulators, customers, employees, and the broader community.
The Board is responsible for the Bank’s strategic direction and is supported by various Board Committees and Executive 
Committees. These Committees operate under clearly defined charters, ensuring focused oversight and effective 
decision-making in their respective domains.

Scheduling the meetings 
The schedule for quarterly meetings of the Board and its Committee

s is finalised well in advance to ensure the availability 
and effective participation of Directors. In cases of exigent business requirements, meetings are convened at shorter notice, 
either in person or via electronic means, or matters are approved through circulation.
Items involving unpublished price-sensitive information are circulated to the Board and Committee members at shorter 
notice, in accordance with the general consent obtained pursuant to the applicable Secretarial Standards from time to time.
Agenda of the meetings
The agenda for Board and Board Committee meetings are prepared in accordance with the Calendar of Reviews, applicable 
laws, and business requirements. Agenda notes are prepared and reviewed by officials of the respective departments in 
consultation with the Functional Head/Company Secretary.
To facilitate effective discussions at the meetings, the agendas are bifurcated into three categories, namely approval, policies, 
and noting/review, to facilitate efficient time management, informed decision-making and active participation, leading to 
higher Board effectiveness.
Procedure
Agendas and presentations for Board and Committee meetings are circulated to Board and Committee members in advance 
via a secure application, with members having unrestricted access to relevant information. The respective senior officials are 
invited to present the agenda items and provide insights to support well-informed decision-making.

Post-meeting action tracker
Directions given by the Board/Committee are communicated to the relevant officials/departments to take necessary action. 
Important decisions taken at the Board and Committee meetings are tracked till their closure, and an Action Taken Report is 
placed before the Board and Committees at their respective meetings.
Minutes of the meeting
Pursuant to the requirements of the Secretarial Standard on Meetings of the Board of Directors (‘SS-1’) issued by the Institute 
of Company Secretaries of India, the draft minutes are circulated to the members of the Board/Committee within 15 days from 
the date of the conclusion of the meetings for their comments. The Comments received from the members on minutes are duly 
incorporated before the minutes are entered in the minutes book. The minutes are subsequently noted at the next meeting. 
The resolution, if any, passed by circulation is placed at the next meeting of the Board/ Committee.

The terms of reference of the Audit Committee, inter-alia, include:

the independence of the Risk Management function.
